en: The Ratnamegha Sūtra, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master Mandarakaśrī of Funan during the Liang Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time the Buddha was staying on the summit of Mount Gayā together with a great assembly of bhikṣus.
There were seventy thousand people together with them—all of whom had completed what was to be done, laid down their heavy burdens, and attained mastery over their own minds;
who had exhausted all fetters of existence and were liberated through right view; who were like great dragons, skillfully understanding the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu);
who were sons of the Dharma, capable of renouncing gain and honor, perfectly endowed with the life of a renunciant, and having properly received full ordination.
All that their hearts desired was fully satisfied, as they dwelt in the path to *nirvāṇa*—with the sole exception of Ānanda, who remained on the stage of a learner (*śaikṣa*).

There were eighty-four thousand great bodhisattvas present, all of whom were in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), advancing toward omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) without regression; they sought the ground of Buddhahood with resolve and drew near to the further shore.

They had attained incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) *dhāraṇīs*, mastered the various *dhyānas* and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, and sported with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*); their great kindness and great compassion pervaded the ten directions, reaching even unto immeasurable and boundless Buddha-lands.
They traverse the realm of emptiness, eliminating all hindrances and obstructions, and exhausting the roots of the three poisons;

they skillfully roam within the abode of signlessness, constantly desiring to rescue and deliver all sentient beings; they have thorough knowledge of the worlds of all Buddhas and have attained unimpeded wisdom.

Their minds are as vast and deep as space and as expansive as the ocean; like Mount Sumeru, they are unmoved by the eight winds; like a lotus flower, their minds are unstained by dust or water; their intentions are like genuine jewels, transparent both inside and out; and like pure, refined gold, they are free from internal flaws or impurities.
Their names were: Bodhisattva Jewel Light,
Bodhisattva Jewel Palm, Bodhisattva Jewel-Sealed Hand, Bodhisattva Jewel Heavenly Crown,
Bodhisattva Jewel Garland, Bodhisattva Jewel Accumulation, Bodhisattva Jewel Treasury, and Bodhisattva Jewel Mountain Peak.
Bodhisattva, Ratnaketu Bodhisattva, Vajragarbha Bodhisattva, Suvarṇagarbha Bodhisattva,
Ratnagarbha Bodhisattva, Puṇyagarbha Bodhisattva, Vimalanirbhāsagarbha Bodhisattva, Tathāgatagarbha Bodhisattva,
Jñānagarbha Bodhisattva, Sūryagarbha Bodhisattva, Samādhi-garbha Bodhisattva, Padma...
The Bodhisattva Padmagarbha, the Bodhisattva Vimukticandra, the Bodhisattva Samantacandra, the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara,
the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra, the Bodhisattva Samantanetra, the Bodhisattva Padmanetra, the Bodhisattva Mahānetra,
the Bodhisattva Samanteryāpatha, the Bodhisattva Samantapratimaṇḍita, and the Bodhisattva Samantacaryā.
The Bodhisattva Jñānasamādhi, the Bodhisattva Dharmamati, the Bodhisattva Vijayamati,
the Bodhisattva Vardhamānamati, the Bodhisattva Vajramati, the Bodhisattva Siṃhavikrāmin,
the Bodhisattva Mahāghoṣarāja, the Bodhisattva Siṃhanādamati, the Bodhisattva Gambhīraghoṣa, and the Bodhisattva Anupalipta.
the Bodhisattva Free from All Defilements, the Bodhisattva Moonlight, the Bodhisattva Sunlight,
the Bodhisattva Wisdom Light, the Bodhisattva Merit of Wisdom, the Bodhisattva Merit of the Moon,
the Bodhisattva Merit of the Lotus, the Bodhisattva Merit of Jewels, the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, and Bhadrapāla and the others.
The sixteen virtuous men, the thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, and others, with Maitreya as their foremost leader;
the gods of the Four Heavenly Kings and others, with the Four Heavenly Kings as their foremost leaders.
Among the gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, Śakra is the foremost;
among the Yāma Heaven, the King of the Yāmas is the foremost;
among the Tuṣita Heaven, the King of the Tuṣitas is the foremost.
Among the gods of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations, the King of the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations is the foremost;
among the gods of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations, the King of the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations is the foremost.
Among the gods of the Good Realm (Śubhakṛtsna), Sadhātva is the foremost;
among all the Brahmā kings, Mahābrahmā is the foremost;
among the gods of the Śuddhāvāsa realm, Maheśvara is the foremost.
The asura kings Vemacitrin, Bali, Rāhu, and so forth—countless hundreds of thousands of billions of asura kings;
the nāga kings Anavatapta, Maṇasvin, Sāgara, Nanda, Vāsuki, and Takṣaka, along with hundreds of thousands of billions of such nāgas, nāga sons, and nāga consorts.

In this manner, hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings—gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans—all these hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings came together for the assembly.
At that time, atop Mount Gayā, an area of four yojanas was completely filled with a great assembly reaching from the tips of needles and the finest motes of dust to the very heavens and the earth.
Lion thrones were spread everywhere, magnificent and radiant, one yojana in height and unsurpassed in their exquisite adornment;
they were half a yojana in width, and eight thousand celestial robes were spread across them.
The ground became entirely level and transformed into vajra; silk banners were suspended, and fragrant liquids were sprinkled upon it, while immeasurable celestial flowers filled the space.

To the left and right of the seat, various lotuses grew, as large as chariot wheels, with hundreds of thousands of millions of petals and stems of pure gold. Their pedestals were made of deep blue lapis lazuli and their filaments of indranīla, fragrant, pure, and pleasing to the mind; they brought joy whenever touched. Such wondrous flowers were used to make offerings to the Buddha.
At each of the four corners of that lion throne grew precious trees fifteen *li* in height, their canopies extending for half a *yojana*.

Upon such a magnificently adorned lion throne sat the Buddha, his mind pure, skillfully turning the wheel of Dharma, subduing the hosts of Māra and his enemies, untainted by the eight worldly dharmas, having attained fearlessness, and possessing unimpeded wisdom and eloquence. His mind was as undaunted as a lion; his mental conduct was as pure as a clear, deep pool; he was as profound and vast as the ocean from which all manner of treasures emerge; he stood like Mount Sumeru amidst the great sea; he was as brilliantly radiant as the sun illuminating all things; he was as full and pure as the moon at its peak; he rained down the great rain of Dharma like a dragon king; and he was exalted and prominent among the assembly like the Great Brahmā.

His immeasurable disciples were all thoroughly disciplined; immeasurable Śakras, Brahmās, and the Four Heavenly Kings gazed upon the Buddha with minds free from pride or inferiority. He was able to cause the great assembly to radiate a warm light like that of the sun, adorned with various jewels.

At that time, the World-Honored One’s physical appearance was radiant and serene, like the sun’s warm illumination upon the entire great assembly; he was like a jewel adorned with ornaments. From the crown of his head, he emitted a light named "Pervasive," which universally illuminated hundreds of thousands of worlds, with immeasurable rays of light as its retinue, simultaneously shining throughout the ten directions. After circling the Buddha three times, the light entered through his mouth, yet there was no change in the appearance of his mouth.
It is like the pure moon clearly illuminating the void, yet the void itself possesses no distinct characteristics;
so too it is with the light entering through the mouth.
It is like a heap of sand into which clarified butter or oil is poured, yet no increase or decrease is perceived.
The Buddha’s light entering his mouth was likewise so.

At that time, to the east, beyond worlds as numerous as the sands of immeasurable Ganges Rivers, there was a land named Lotus Sovereignty (*Padma-vaśavartin*). In that world dwelt a Buddha named Padmanetra Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavat, who was teaching the Dharma of the Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*) to the bodhisattvas.
In that land, there are no names for śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas.
At that time, all sentient beings attain the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika) and advance toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
These sentient beings have no food of morsels; they subsist solely on the food of the joy of the Dharma and the delight of dhyāna.
Although that land possesses suns, moons, and stars, these do not provide illumination; only the light of the Buddha shines upon that realm.
It is devoid of mountains, forests, stumps, or thorns, and its ground is as level as the palm of a hand.
In that realm there was a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin; upon hearing his name, all karmic obstructions were entirely eliminated.

At that time, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, having been touched by the light, went immediately to the presence of the Buddha Padmanetra. He prostrated with his head to the ground before the Buddha as a mark of reverence, then withdrew to sit to one side upon a lotus flower.

Furthermore, immeasurable bodhisattvas, having been graced by the light, also went to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves with their heads at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"By what causes and conditions does this radiance exist?
Those who encounter this light find their minds and thoughts filled with joy; from where does such light come?
The Buddha Padmanetra replied:

“Good son! To the west there is a world named Sahā, where the Buddha is known as Śākyamuni Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān. Upon hearing the name of that Buddha, all attain the stage of Avaivartika; it is from that Buddha that such light is emitted.”
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions do all who hear the name of that Buddha attain the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*) and advance toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*?”
The Buddha Padmanetra further addressed the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, saying:
"When that Buddha was practicing the bodhisattva path, he made this great vow:
'If I attain buddhahood, may all who hear my name resolve their minds toward anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and attain the stage of avaivartika.'"
The Bodhisattva Nivāraṇaviṣkambhin again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If those who hear the name of that Buddha all resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* and attain the stage of *avaivartika*, have all the sentient beings in that land already attained this?”
The Buddha Padmanetra replied:
"Good son, there is attainment and non-attainment."
The Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Will the sentient beings of that land not hear it?"
The Buddha Padmanetra replied,
“Good son, you shall also hear his name.”
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If it is as you have heard, how can there be attainment and non-attainment?”
The Buddha Padmanetra replied,
“Good son! The sentient beings in that land are all non-retrogressive (avaivartika), yet they are also not non-retrogressive.”
The Bodhisattva Avaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
why is it that all these are both *avaivartika* and yet not *avaivartika*?”
The Buddha Padmanetra replied: "Good son!

Those who hear the name of that Buddha, although they obtain the causal conditions for the seed of *avaivartika*, do not receive a prediction of enlightenment because their practice is incomplete and not yet fulfilled."
"Good son!
I shall now speak a parable for you.
Suppose there were a tree being planted; its seed is free from decay and possesses all the conditions necessary for the sprout to grow. Should one say that it will grow, or that it will not grow?"
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
This is called birth.”
The Buddha Padmanetra replied, “Good son!
Those who hear the name of the Buddha obtain its seed; when the requisite conditions are fulfilled, they shall receive their prediction of enlightenment.”
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
I wish to go to the Sahā world to pay homage and show reverence to Śākyamuni Buddha.”
The Buddha Padmanetra immediately replied:
"Good son! Now is precisely the right time; you may go to pay him homage."
Those bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
We, too, shall follow the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin to go to the Sahā world to pay homage, show reverence, honor, and praise him.”
The Buddha Padmanetra addressed the bodhisattvas, saying:
"Now is the very time; you may go to him.
Do not give rise to thoughts of inferiority or negligence."

Why is this? Because the sentient beings in that realm abound in greed, anger, and delusion; they are unwilling to show reverence to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; they delight in practicing what is unrighteous; their minds are coarse and debased; they use foul language and revile others; they are stubborn, perverse, and difficult to discipline; they are stingy, greedy, envious, and jealous; they are indolent, lazy, negligent, and violate the precepts; they are bound and entangled by immeasurable afflictions.
It is among such beings in the midst of evil births that he preaches the Dharma.
At that time, those bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Śākyamuni Buddha is most rare and extraordinary, for he is able to preach the Dharma among the sentient beings of that evil world.”
The Buddha Padmanetra replied:
"Good son! That Blessed One is truly rare and marvelous."
As you have said, one must dwell among sentient beings who are constantly in evil states and expound the Dharma for them.
It is likewise rare for anyone in such an evil world to give rise to even a single thought of a wholesome mind.
Why is this? In pure worlds, it is not difficult for sentient beings to maintain faith and cultivate goodness;

however, in evil worlds, to give rise to a mind of faith and take refuge in the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha in the space of a finger-snap; to be able to practice and uphold the precepts in the space of a finger-snap; to give rise to a mind free from desire in the space of a finger-snap; and to give rise to compassion and resolve to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* in the space of a finger-snap—this is exceedingly difficult.
The bodhisattvas addressed the Buddha, saying:
“It is marvelous,
World-Honored One!”
"How marvelous!
Well-gone One!
At that time, among all the bodhisattvas, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin was the foremost leader.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin and all the other bodhisattvas, having received the Buddha’s instruction, were filled with joy and exultation;
they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and each returned to their original seat.

These bodhisattvas brought various jewel trees, complete with flowers and fruits—some brought beryl trees, some brought crystal trees, some brought gold trees, some brought trees of manifold jewels, some brought flower trees, and some brought fruit trees; some brought clouds of garments, some brought rings, bracelets, and necklaces, some brought clouds of incense, some brought clouds of flower garlands, some brought clouds of precious parasols, some brought clouds of precious banners and pennants, and some brought clouds of music—all of whom gathered at the place of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin and together proceeded to the Sahā world.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the assembly of bodhisattvas, saying:
"In that Sahā world, sentient beings undergo much suffering and affliction; each of you should manifest your supernormal powers so that those beings may attain happiness."
Then all the bodhisattvas replied, "So be it. At that time,

the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, through his supernormal powers, emitted light from his body— pure and stainless— which illuminated the entire Sahā world-system of three thousand great thousandfold worlds.

This light is able to illuminate the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and King Yama; those suffering from various afflictions who are touched by this light experience physical bliss, and their greed and hatred are entirely extinguished, so that they regard one another with a heart of loving-kindness, as if toward their own parents.

In all the dark and gloomy places within the trichiliocosm, where the light of the sun, the moon, and other luminaries cannot reach, all are able to see one another by means of the Bodhisattva’s radiance.

Within the trichiliocosm, the regions of darkness among the Cakravāḍa Mountains, Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, Mucilinda Mountains, Mahāmucilinda Mountains, and all other mountains are entirely illumined by this light.
From the Brahma Heaven above down to the Avīci Hell below, the intermediate space is thus universally bathed in radiance.

Furthermore, all the bodhisattvas emitted light from their bodies; those who encountered this light had their various sufferings entirely eliminated: the hungry received food, the thirsty received drink, the naked received clothing, the poor received wealth, the blind were able to see, the deaf were able to hear, the mute were able to speak, the lame were able to walk, the insane regained their composure, and the suffering found happiness. Moreover, all women who were pregnant were enabled to give birth in peace and safety. At that time, all manner of suffering was utterly removed.

Together with all the bodhisattvas, he arrived simultaneously at the summit of Mount Gayā. A net of jewels covered the entire trichiliocosm. In the void of space, clouds of lotuses rained down lotuses;

clouds of exquisite fruits rained down exquisite fruits; clouds of flower garlands rained down flower garlands; clouds of incense rained down incense; clouds of white cotton cloth rained down white cotton cloth; clouds of powdered incense rained down powdered incense; clouds of robes rained down robes; clouds of precious canopies rained down precious canopies; clouds of precious banners rained down precious banners; and clouds of precious pennants rained down precious pennants. These various clouds rained down according to their respective kinds, and when they touched the body, there was softness and bliss.

At that time, the pits, hollows, and mounds of Mount Gayā became naturally level; all the mountains and trees were transformed into jewel groves, appearing as sandalwood, aloeswood, and various fragrant trees, which adorned the surroundings everywhere.
A hundred thousand celestial musical instruments resounded spontaneously in the void without being struck, and from amidst those musical sounds, these verses emerged together:
"Born in the Vipula forest, Not arising from the bonds of karma,
Unrivaled and peerless— To him I now pay homage."
With a mind as level as space, having reached Mount Gayā,
I now take refuge in the most wondrous, supreme, and unsurpassed Bodhi.
Sitting beneath the tree of enlightenment, I have finally realized perfect awakening.
Pointing to the earth as witness, all Māras and adversaries were made to retreat and disperse;
I now arrive at Gayā and prostrate before the Stainless Honored One.
All that exists in the world is an illusion and transformation, just like foam, bubbles, and a mirage.
Deceptive as the moon reflected in water, the characteristics of phenomena are likewise so; having now come here, I pay homage to the Tree of Right Wisdom.
Just as a master of the arts can manifest all manner of skillful transformations, [so too does the Buddha appear].
The various dharmas are manifold, like the crimson of a celestial horse;
I bow my head in homage to the Immovable One, the treasury of merit.
Having now come from him, I pay respectful salutation to the Unsurpassed Honored One.
Having deeply given rise to great compassion, For immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas,
Cultivating morality, concentration, and wisdom, And accumulating all manner of wholesome deeds,
I have now come from there To pay homage to your pure moon-like face.
Hundreds of billions of bodhisattvas and immeasurable hosts of devas all came from that place to pay homage to the Honored One who Dispels Darkness;
having obtained the Dharma-treasury, he expounded it for the sake of the multitude out of compassion.
The one who is able to bring benefit is the most peerless Honored One;
having come from him, I now bow my head to the Perfectly Awakened One.
With compassion he rescues all sentient beings; he is tranquil and serene.
As a lotus is not stained by water, so my mind is undefiled by afflictions;
I now come to take refuge and pay homage to this one of supreme virtue.
Your pure body is free from stain, and its various marks are like blossoming flowers.
The eighty minor marks are the fruit; having become a refuge for the world,
I have now come from there to bow my head before the jewel tree,
which possesses immeasurable branches and twigs, and which we all worship.
At that time, the Venerable Maudgalyāyana rose from his seat, knelt with palms joined, bared his right shoulder, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"I now do not see his form, yet I hear these various wonderful verses.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:

"To the east, beyond immeasurable *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* buddha-fields, there is a world-system called Padmāvatī. There dwells a Buddha named Padmaviśuddhanetra, who is currently preaching the Dharma for a great assembly."

In that realm there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, along with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of other bodhisattvas, who have all come to this Sahā world desiring to pay homage and show reverence to me, and to listen to the Dharma with a sincere mind; it was those bodhisattvas who composed these verses.

When the Buddha had finished speaking, those bodhisattvas immediately went before the Buddha; with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin as their leader, they all together prostrated themselves, touching their heads to the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to stand to one side. Joining their palms toward the Buddha, they praised him in verse:
"Homage to the one of great renown, To the one endowed with perfect wisdom;
Homage to the one of great diligence, To the most supreme Muni."
Able to uproot the three realms of existence, Crossing over to the far shore beyond afflictions,
With divine light illuminating the world, I take refuge in the Peerless Honored One.
The four quarters receive the radiance of his light, And all are universally liberated.
I take refuge in the one of incomparable renown, Unshakable as the king of mountains;
As deep and vast as the great ocean, His wisdom is immeasurable.
None among all the non-Buddhists Are able to disturb or confound him.
I now prostrate in homage, taking refuge in the Dharma King.
The foremost path of quiescence, neither arising nor ceasing,
Its essence and characteristics like nirvāṇa— I take refuge in the Dharma King who preaches it.
One who is able to turn the wheel of Dharma manifests the right path,
abides in the true reality, expounds upon nirvāṇa,
bestows the prediction of enlightenment, and thoroughly understands the characteristics of phenomena.
As well as the nature of the afflictions, one should practice according to what has been taught.
One observes the discipline [and sees] greed, all forms of hatred,
the immeasurable stains of the mind, and all the obstructions of the sensory dusts.
Beneath the Bodhi tree, the fire of wisdom has completely consumed [all defilements];
He delivers all sentient beings, saving himself and saving others.
Within the vast wilderness of birth and death, he strives to rescue all living beings.
Long have you slumbered in profound darkness, bound by the prisons of the three realms of existence.
I urge you to awaken early and turn toward the place of refuge;
I shall act as your kinsman and friend until the very end, so that you may never again fall into heedlessness.
"Those who have followed me here all abide in Bodhi;
desiring to hear the True Dharma, I pray that you will explain it at this time.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin had praised the Buddha with these verses, the Buddha addressed the bodhisattvas:
"Each of you return to your original seats.
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin and all the other bodhisattvas then sat upon lotus pedestals.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to ask a question; I only pray that you will grant me leave.
The Buddha then replied:
“If there are those who have doubts, ask whatever you wish, and I shall analyze and explain it for you.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

How does a bodhisattva become fully endowed with generosity, fully endowed with ethical discipline, fully endowed with patience, fully endowed with diligence, fully endowed with meditative concentration, fully endowed with wisdom, fully endowed with skillful means, fully endowed with aspiration, fully endowed with power, and fully endowed with knowledge?
How is it that a bodhisattva is equal to earth?
How is it that a bodhisattva is equal to water?
How is it that a bodhisattva is equal to fire?
How is it that a bodhisattva is equal to space?
How is it that a bodhisattva is like the moon?
How is it that a bodhisattva is like the sun?
How is it that a bodhisattva is like a lion?
How is it that a bodhisattva is well-tamed?
How is it that a bodhisattva is a skilled charioteer?
How is it that a bodhisattva is like a lotus?
How does a bodhisattva attain a great mind?
How does a bodhisattva attain a pure mind?
How does a bodhisattva attain a mind free from the net of doubt?
How is a bodhisattva as profound as the great ocean?
How does a bodhisattva attain subtle wisdom?
How does a bodhisattva attain eloquence that is compliant?
How does a bodhisattva attain inexhaustible eloquence?
How does a bodhisattva attain pure eloquence?
How does a bodhisattva enable sentient beings to attain few desires and contentment?
How does a bodhisattva attain responsive eloquence?
How does a bodhisattva act as a Dharma teacher?
How does a bodhisattva attain accordance with the Dharma?
How does a bodhisattva achieve skillful understanding of the dharma-realm?
How does a bodhisattva practice within the sphere of emptiness?
How does a bodhisattva practice the realm of signlessness?
How does a bodhisattva practice the realm of wishlessness?
How does a bodhisattva practice loving-kindness?
How does a bodhisattva practice compassion?
How does a bodhisattva practice sympathetic joy?
How does a bodhisattva practice equanimity?
How does a bodhisattva attain the supernormal powers of playful mastery?
How does a bodhisattva attain freedom from the eight difficult conditions?
How does a bodhisattva attain the non-forgetfulness of the bodhicitta?
How does a bodhisattva attain the knowledge of past lives?
How does a bodhisattva never be separated from spiritual friends?
How does a bodhisattva become free from evil associates?
How does a bodhisattva attain the pure body of a Buddha?
How does a bodhisattva attain a vajra-body?
How does a bodhisattva become a great caravan leader?
How does a bodhisattva attain thorough knowledge of all paths?
How does a bodhisattva show the non-perverted path?
How does a bodhisattva constantly maintain a concentrated mind?
How does a bodhisattva obtain rag-robes?
How does a bodhisattva obtain the three robes?
How does a bodhisattva obtain *kāṣāya* robes?
How does a bodhisattva obtain the practice of begging for food?
How does a bodhisattva obtain the practice of eating in a single sitting?
How does a bodhisattva obtain the practice of receiving food only once?
How does a bodhisattva obtain non-food as food?
How does a bodhisattva obtain the practice of forest-dwelling (āraṇyaka)?
How does a bodhisattva obtain sitting at the foot of a tree?
How does a bodhisattva attain the practice of sitting in the open air?
How does a bodhisattva practice dwelling among burial mounds?
How does a bodhisattva remain constantly seated without lying down?
How does a bodhisattva sit according to the arrangement of seats?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully know the methods for instructing in dhyāna?
How does a bodhisattva maintain the sūtras?
How does a bodhisattva uphold the Vinaya-piṭaka?
How does a bodhisattva maintain dignified deportment?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully know the places where one may go?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully know the method of practice?
How does a bodhisattva eliminate greed and envy?
How does a bodhisattva give rise to a mind of equanimity toward all sentient beings?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully know how to make offerings to the Tathāgata?
How does a bodhisattva eliminate arrogance?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully attain a mind of faith and reverence?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully understand the ultimate truth?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully know the twelve links of dependent origination?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully know the essential nature and characteristics of the self?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully know the characteristics of the world?
How does a bodhisattva give birth in a pure buddha-field?
How does a bodhisattva remain undefiled while dwelling in the womb?
How does a bodhisattva leave home and go forth into homelessness?
How does a bodhisattva attain a pure livelihood?
How does a bodhisattva’s mind remain free from sorrow and affliction?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully follow the Buddha’s teachings?
How does a bodhisattva always speak with a serene countenance and abandon frowning?
How does a bodhisattva become fully endowed with extensive learning?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully uphold the true Dharma?
How does a bodhisattva become a prince of the Dharma?
How does a bodhisattva receive offerings from the Four Heavenly Kings, Śakra, and Brahmā?
How does a bodhisattva know the essential characteristics of others?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully know how to bring sentient beings to maturity?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully cultivate the practice of gentleness?
How does a bodhisattva dwell in communal harmony and peace?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully cultivate the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*)?
How does a bodhisattva attain dignified and upright deportment (*īryāpatha*)?
How does a bodhisattva skillfully serve as a place of reliance for sentient beings?
How is a bodhisattva like a medicinal tree?
How does a bodhisattva constantly cultivate all forms of goodness?
"How does a bodhisattva skillfully perform transformations?
How does a bodhisattva mahāsattva swiftly attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?
The Buddha addressed the bodhisattva mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin:
“Excellent, excellent, son of good family!
Because you wish to benefit gods and humans and to deliver all sentient beings, you have posed this question; I shall now explain it for you.”
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Excellent, World-Honored One!
We pray that you will expound this at this time.”
The Buddha then addressed them, saying: "Good sons!
I shall now speak; listen attentively."
“A bodhisattva who accomplishes ten dharmas is able to fulfill dāna. What are these ten? Fulfillment of the gift of Dharma;

fulfillment of the gift of fearlessness; fulfillment of the gift of material wealth; fulfillment of the gift without expectation of reward; fulfillment of the gift of compassion; fulfillment of the gift with a mind free from contempt; fulfillment of the gift of reverence; fulfillment of the gift of respectful service; fulfillment of the gift that does not seek existence; and fulfillment of the pure gift.”
“Good son! What is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of the gift of Dharma?

It is to uphold the Dharma oneself and expound it for others with a mind free from expectation, seeking neither gain nor profit, nor fame; doing so to eliminate the faults and evils of all sentient beings, and not for the sake of personal advantage.”

With a mind free from high or low, he preaches the Dharma with equanimity; whether preaching for kings, those equal to kings, or even for caṇḍālas, he does so with complete equality and without distinction.
One does not become arrogant or conceited because of this giving.
If one can act in this way, it is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the gift of Dharma.
What is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the gift of fearlessness?
The Bodhisattva personally refrains from weapons and staves, and also teaches others to refrain from weapons and staves.
Toward all sentient beings, they conceive the thought of them as their parents, as sons and daughters, or as kinsmen and friends.
Why is this? The Buddha has taught that among all sentient beings, from beginningless kalpas, there are none who have not been one's father, mother, son, or daughter.
A bodhisattva constantly gives away their own body even for the most minute of beings, let alone for other great multitudes of sentient beings.
This is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the gift of fearlessness.
What is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the gift of material wealth?

When a Bodhisattva sees sentient beings committing many evil deeds, he accumulates wealth and treasures to bestow upon them, causing them to abandon their evil karma and establish them in wholesome states.

Furthermore, I have heard the Buddha, the World-Honored One, speak thus: "Generosity (dāna) is that by which a bodhisattva can remove the defilements of stinginess, greed, and envy; as the Buddha has taught, one should practice giving, yet not allow the mind to become arrogant on account of such giving."
This is called the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the gift of material wealth.
What is meant by the Bodhisattva’s fulfillment of giving without expectation of reward?
It is not giving for the sake of gaining followers, nor giving for the sake of gaining friends, nor giving out of desire; rather, the Bodhisattva gives with this reflection:
“The pure precepts of a bodhisattva are a practice that is constant.
For this reason, it is called the bodhisattva’s perfection of giving without expectation of reward.
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s perfection of giving through the accomplishment of compassion?

When a bodhisattva sees sentient beings suffering from hunger and thirst, naked or clad in tattered rags, without anyone to rely upon, without refuge, without a destination, without a dwelling place, and devoid of meritorious deeds, he gives rise to a profound and compassionate mind, thinking:

"It is for the sake of these suffering sentient beings that I have now resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Yet these beings continue to revolve in saṃsāra, enduring suffering, naked or clad in tattered rags, without reliance, without refuge, without a destination, and afflicted by hunger and cold. When shall I provide for these beings clothing and food, even providing them with a home as a place of refuge?"

"Whatever wealth and goods he currently possesses, he gives them all away; yet, although he performs such giving, he does not give rise to thoughts of a self, a person, or the notion that there are such things as 'wealth' and 'goods.
Giving in this manner is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of compassionate giving."
“What is meant by a bodhisattva’s perfection of giving with an undiscouraged mind?

It is giving without discrimination; giving with equal great compassion; giving with an undiscouraged mind; giving without stinginess of heart; giving without anger or resentment; giving without arrogance or negligence; giving not for the sake of gaining fame; and giving not because of the thought ‘I am learned. Such giving as this is called giving with single-minded devotion, giving with reverence, giving with respect, and giving with one’s own hands.”
Giving such as this is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of giving with a mind free from contempt.
What is called the Bodhisattva’s perfection of giving through service?

It refers to those of shared religious practice who are worthy of honor and service—such as preceptors (*upādhyāya*), instructors (*ācārya*), and the like—toward whom one generates profound reverence, rising to meet them, joining the palms in greeting, looking up with respect, and personally assisting them in whatever tasks they undertake.
Giving in this manner is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the gift of service.
What is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of the gift of reverence?
It is making offerings to the Buddha, making offerings to the Dharma, and making offerings to the Sangha.
To circumambulate the Tathāgata’s stūpa with incense, flowers, and music; to smear and sweep the ground of the Buddha’s site;
and to repair, restore, and adorn any stūpas or temples that have become dilapidated or collapsed—this is called honoring the Buddha.

To revere the Dharma means to listen to it, read and recite it, receive and uphold it, copy it, explain it, contemplate its meaning, practice according to the Dharma, and grasp its meaning without error; this is called revering the Dharma.

To revere the Saṃgha means to provide and offer to the Saṃgha whatever is required—robes, food and drink, bedding, medicinal decoctions, and various miscellaneous items—even when one is so impoverished as to possess nothing at all, one should respectfully offer pure water with a reverent heart;
such giving is called "the gift of revering the Saṃgha."
If one can make offerings to the Three Jewels in this manner, it is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of respectful giving.
What is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of giving without seeking existence?
When a bodhisattva practices giving, they do not give rise to the thought:
"I shall be reborn in heaven," nor do they give rise to the thought:
"I shall become a king, along with various ministers, high officials, and subordinate functionaries.
This is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of giving without seeking existence.
What is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of pure giving?
When a bodhisattva contemplates this giving as being stainless, undefiled, and unmixed, such a giver is said to be a bodhisattva who is fully endowed with pure giving. "Good son!
One who possesses these ten matters is said to be a bodhisattva fully endowed with dāna. "Good son,
there are further ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva achieves pure śīla."

What are the ten? They are: being well-trained in the *prātimokṣa* precepts; being well-maintained in the subtle and detailed bodhisattva precepts; extinguishing all afflictions (*kleśa*); eliminating unwholesome thoughts; fearing evil karma; feeling awe and dread even toward minor offenses; maintaining a mind that is constantly apprehensive [of transgression]; firmly upholding the *dhūta* practices without deficiency; not undertaking the observance of precepts for the sake of creating karma for rebirth in existence; and purifying the three types of action (*trikarma*).
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s skillful training in the *prātimokṣa* precepts?

A bodhisattva single-mindedly receives and upholds all the precept scriptures established by the Buddha; they do not observe the precepts for the sake of lineage, nor do they observe them for the sake of the view of self, nor do they observe them for the sake of gathering a following, nor do they disparage the precepts upon seeing the faults of others.
This is called a bodhisattva’s skillful observance of the *prātimokṣa* precepts."
"What is meant by a bodhisattva skillfully maintaining the dense and subtle precepts?
A bodhisattva reflects thus:

'It is not only the prātimokṣa precepts that can enable me to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; I must also study and practice in accordance with the Dharma all other bodhisattva rules of conduct and disciplinary observances.'"

"What is the Bodhisattva precept? A bodhisattva never goes to places where they ought not to go; they do not speak at improper times. They skillfully know the seasons and skillfully understand local customs, acting in accordance with the hearts of others so as not to cause sentient beings to give rise to criticism or suspicion. They skillfully protect sentient beings, leading them to Bodhi, while also personally fulfilling the majestic deportment of Bodhi. Their speech is gentle and they speak sparingly; they do not enjoy associating with high ministers or officials, but constantly cultivate the practice of *āraṇya* (forest dwelling) with a serene countenance and a pleasant expression."

To be able to fully possess such bodhisattva deportment and precepts, as well as all other bodhisattva precepts found in various sūtras and to practice them completely—this is called the bodhisattva’s meticulous precepts.
"What is meant by 'the Bodhisattva extinguishes all fetters so that they are entirely scorched'?
It means that greed, anger, delusion, and all other entanglements and obstacles, as well as all material requisites, are likewise entirely scorched."
One gives rise to counteractive dharmas regarding the objects of sensual desire, whereby all that can give rise to desire is completely severed.
What are the objects of sensual desire?
They are the conditions that can give rise to desire with respect to beautiful forms.
What is called the perception of impurity? It is as follows:

when one contemplates one’s own body—its hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, blood, flesh, tendons, veins, bones, marrow, sweat, tears, nasal mucus, saliva, fat, grease, brain, membranes, throat, esophagus, heart, gallbladder, liver, lungs, spleen, kidneys, intestines, stomach, hundred vessels, raw intestines, cooked intestines, excrement, urine, and pus—the Bodhisattva constantly contemplates these thirty-six items; if one can do so, no mind of greed will arise.

If even fools, infants, or those with deranged minds and distracted thoughts do not give rise to thoughts of desire upon seeing these thirty-six things, how much less would the wise ones—the various bodhisattvas—who constantly contemplate this impurity, ever again give rise to thoughts of desire?
When a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva sees a beloved form that is pleasing to the mind and a defiled thought arises, at the very moment of first seeing that form, he reflects to himself:
"As the Buddha has taught, form is like a dream or an echo; it possesses no substantial reality."
"How can a wise person falsely give rise to thoughts of desire within a dream?
For this reason, a bodhisattva is able to distance themselves from all places where desire arises.
How does a bodhisattva give rise to remedial dharmas toward that which provokes anger, thereby being able to leave behind both hatred and its causal conditions?
A bodhisattva constantly gives rise to a mind of loving-kindness toward all sentient beings; by this causal condition, they are able to eliminate anger.
If anger should arise due to conditions of affliction or harm, one should deeply fix the mind upon the methods of counteraction; this is called the bodhisattva’s skillful means for eliminating anger.
What is the bodhisattva’s skillful means for eliminating delusion?
One should reflect:
"The deluded mind does not distinguish between good and evil; it constantly abides in ignorant darkness and later undergoes the fruits of suffering."
"Lacking wisdom, one obscures oneself; causing distress to others, one has few conditions for success. This is not as [severe] as greed and anger, which bring much enmity and harm.
When one contemplates in this way, the mind of delusion is extinguished; this is called the Bodhisattva’s scorching of afflictions.
"What is meant by 'the bodhisattva's elimination of unwholesome thoughts'?
Abiding in a secluded and quiet forest hermitage (*aranyaka*), one forms this thought:
'I have now distanced myself from places of clamor and bustle; in this tranquil place, I practice the Buddha’s teachings.'"
"Other śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas associate with the clamor and bustle of crowds, which brings much disturbance and leads them away from the Buddha’s teaching.
This is called the bodhisattva’s elimination of unwholesome thoughts.
"What is meant by 'a bodhisattva’s dread of evil karma'?
It means observing and discerning what the Buddha has previously taught, single-mindedly cultivating merit, firmly upholding pure precepts, and skillfully training in wisdom."
For what reason does one obtain the most excellent retribution?
By possessing meritorious karma and remaining far removed from all evils.
This is called a bodhisattva’s dread of evil karma.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva fearing even minor evils?
It means that regarding even small transgressions, one constantly gives rise to a mind of great fear, never treating even the slightest evil with contempt.
For what reason?"
I have heard the Buddha say:
"A small amount of poison can kill a person; how much more so a large amount?
Even among subtle evils, one can still be led to the three evil realms; how much more so when there is great evil and yet the mind feels no fear?"
This is called a bodhisattva’s dread of even minor evils.
What is meant by a bodhisattva whose mind is always fearful?

Because he is a person of integrity and trustworthiness, when brahmins, kṣatriyas, householders, and others—out of their own integrity and trust—entrust him with gold, silver, and various kinds of precious jewels, paying him with confidence and not establishing a formal written receipt, the bodhisattva never gives rise to a thought of concealment.

Regarding the property of the Buddha, the property of the Dharma, the property of the Saṃgha, or the property of the Saṃgha from the four quarters, a bodhisattva would rather eat his own flesh than ever encroach upon what belongs to others; whether it be drink or food, he does not dare to recklessly destroy any article used for the sustenance of the body. This is called the bodhisattva’s mind being constantly filled with dread and apprehension.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva’s firm and unimpaired upholding of the dhūta practices?

If the retinues of Māra and various devas should come to disturb and coerce the bodhisattva with exquisite wealth, forms, and desires, the bodhisattva immediately remains firm in resolve and unmoved, their mind not being corrupted. This is called a bodhisattva’s firm and unimpaired upholding of the dhūta practices."
"What is meant by 'a bodhisattva upholds the precepts without performing actions for the sake of seeking existence'?

A bodhisattva upholds the precepts not to seek worldly retribution, but solely to fulfill all wholesome dharmas and attain the unsurpassed path; this is called a bodhisattva upholding the precepts without performing actions for the sake of seeking existence."
"What is meant by a bodhisattva purifying the three karmas?
How does one purify bodily karma?
By abstaining from killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct; for this reason, it is called the purification of bodily karma."
How does one purify verbal karma?
By abstaining from harsh speech, false speech, divisive speech, and frivolous speech; for this reason, it is called the purification of verbal karma.
How does one purify mental karma?
To eliminate greed, hatred, delusion, and false views is called purifying the mental action.
This is what is meant by a bodhisattva purifying the three actions. "Good son!
One who possesses these ten matters is said to be a bodhisattva who has accomplished pure ethical discipline.
"Good son, furthermore,
there are ten further dharmas by which a bodhisattva mahāsattva can purify patience."
What are the ten? They are:

internal patience, external patience, patience regarding the Dharma, patience in accordance with the Buddha’s teachings, patience that is not localized, patience cultivated in all places, patience that is not for a specific purpose, patience free from affliction, patience born of compassion, and patience of vow.
"What is called the bodhisattva’s internal forbearance?

When a bodhisattva encounters hunger, thirst, cold, heat, sorrow, grief, pain, or piercing afflictions of body and mind, they are able to endure these things for themselves without being distressed; this is called the bodhisattva’s internal forbearance."
"What is called the bodhisattva’s patience toward external objects?

When a bodhisattva hears from others abusive words, insults, slanders, or defamation—whether directed at their parents, brothers, sisters, relatives, preceptors (*upādhyāya*), teachers (*ācārya*), masters, or fellow students; or whether they hear such things disparaging the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Sangha—the bodhisattva practices patience and does not give rise to anger. This is called the bodhisattva’s patience toward external objects."
"What is called the Bodhisattva’s patience regarding dharmas (*dharmakṣānti*)?
The Buddha has taught the subtle meaning in various sūtras:
'All dharmas are quiescent; all dharmas are extinguished, having the characteristic of nirvāṇa.'"
Without being startled or terrified, the bodhisattva reflects thus:
"If I do not understand this sutra and do not know this Dharma, I shall ultimately never attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."
Therefore, when a bodhisattva diligently seeks out, inquires about, reads, and recites [the teachings], this is called the bodhisattva’s patience regarding the Dharma (*dharmakṣānti*).
What is called the bodhisattva’s patience in accordance with the Buddha’s teaching (*buddhānuśāsany-avakrānti-kṣānti*)?
When a bodhisattva gives rise to a mind of anger, vexation, or poison, they reflect thus:
"From what is this body born?
By what does it perish?"
Regarding that which arises from me, what is "me"?
Regarding that which arises from that, what is "that"? Such being the nature of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), by what causes and conditions do they arise?

When the Bodhisattva engaged in this reflection, he did not perceive anything from which [phenomena] arise, nor did he perceive anything conditioned by objects; he did not perceive them as arising from a self, nor did he perceive them as originating from another, nor did he perceive them as arising from causes and conditions.

Reflecting in this way, one neither becomes angry, nor vexed, nor malicious; thus, the mind of resentment and anger is immediately diminished. This is called the bodhisattva’s patience in accordance with the Buddha's teaching.
"What is called the bodhisattva’s patience that is without fixed location?

It may be that one is patient at night but not by day, or patient by day but not at night; or patient in that place but not in this place, or patient in this place but not in that place; or patient in the presence of acquaintances but not in their absence, or patient in the absence of acquaintances but not in their presence."
The Bodhisattva is not like that; at all times and in all places, they constantly give rise to a mind of patience. This is called the Bodhisattva’s patience that is without fixed location.
What is meant by the Bodhisattva practicing patience in every situation?

There are those who give rise to patience toward parents, teachers and elders, spouses, men and women, the elderly and the young, or those internal and external to their circle, yet do not exercise such patience toward others.

The patience of a bodhisattva is not like this; they cultivate patience toward their parents and likewise toward a candāla. This is called the bodhisattva’s cultivation of patience in all circumstances.
"What is called the bodhisattva’s patience that is not for the sake of anything?

It is patience that does not arise for the sake of some matter, nor for the sake of profit, nor out of fear, nor because of having received a favor from another, nor because of intimacy with a friend, nor out of shame or embarrassment. The bodhisattva constantly cultivates patience; this is called the bodhisattva’s patience that is not for the sake of anything."
“Good son! What is called the bodhisattva’s patience of non-affliction?
If the causes and conditions for anger and the afflictions have not yet arisen, it is not called patience.

If, when encountering the conditions for anger—such as being struck with fists, beaten with knives or staves, kicked or trampled by hands and feet, or reviled with harsh speech—one’s mind remains unmoved therein, this is called patience (*kṣānti*).
If someone comes to provoke anger in a bodhisattva, he endures it; if no one provokes anger, he also endures it. This is called the bodhisattva’s patience of non-affliction.
"What is called the bodhisattva’s patience of compassion?
At that time, whether the bodhisattva acts as a king or one equal to a king, having achieved great meritorious deeds, he serves as a lord for the sake of suffering sentient beings."
When these suffering sentient beings come to revile, insult, or provoke him, the Bodhisattva does not give rise to anger on account of his status as their master, thinking:
"I must rescue and constantly protect such sentient beings; how could I possibly give rise to anger or affliction?"
"Therefore, out of compassion and pity, I do not give rise to anger.
This is called the bodhisattva’s patience of compassionate heart.
"What is called the bodhisattva’s patience of vow?"
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"In the presence of all Buddhas, I have previously uttered the lion's roar and made this vow:
'I shall attain Buddhahood and, from within the mire of all birth and death, I will pull out all sentient beings who suffer.'"
"I now wish to uproot [this affliction]; I should not harbor anger or cause distress to others.
If I cannot endure it myself, I shall not even save myself, let alone benefit sentient beings."

"Good son! It is like a skilled physician who is well-versed in treating the eyes. He sees that many sentient beings suffer from eye ailments—some suffering from cataracts, some from film over the eyes, and various other eye disorders beyond counting."
If that physician were to say,
"I wish to cure the eye ailments of sentient beings," yet at that time the physician himself subsequently became blind.
The Buddha asked,
"Can such a physician treat the eyes of others?
The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Nīvaranaviskambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"No, World-Honored One!
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin:
"One who wishes to dispel the darkness of ignorance for all sentient beings should first eliminate their own obscurations and only thereafter attend to others.
It is not possible that one who lacks internal wisdom can cure the ailments of others."
For these reasons, one should cultivate patience and should not give rise to anger; this is called the Bodhisattva’s patience of the great vow.
"Good son! Possessing these ten matters is what is called a Bodhisattva being able to purify patience."
“Good son! Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva is said to have perfected diligence.
What are these ten?

Vajra-like diligence, incomparable diligence, central diligence, manifestly superior diligence, blazing diligence, constant and perpetual diligence, pure diligence, diligence not shared with the two vehicles, diligence that does not treat others with contempt, and non-retrogressive diligence.
“What is the vajra-like diligence of a bodhisattva?

It is to cause those who have not understood to understand; to cause those who have not attained nirvāṇa to attain nirvāṇa; to cause those who are not settled to be settled; to cause those who have not crossed over to cross over; and to cause those who have not attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”
When one practices with such diligence, the Māra Pāpīyān comes and says to the Bodhisattva:
"Why do you now exert yourself with such diligence?"
To labor in vain will yield no fruit in the end. Why is this? I too have once practiced such diligence:

to cause those who did not understand to understand; to cause those who had not attained *nirvāṇa* to attain *nirvāṇa*; to cause those who were not at peace to find peace; to cause those who had not crossed over to cross over; and to cause all who had not attained *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* to attain it.

Such matters as these are all false speech; they merely deceive the foolish and ignorant and possess no reality. I have never seen anyone who attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi through such diligent effort.
"Good son!
I have seen immeasurable sentient beings who, through such diligence, attained the nirvana of an arhat; and others who, through such diligence, attained the nirvana of a pratyekabuddha."
The Mara King spoke again: "Good son!
Although you practice with diligence, you have not yet attained Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi."
Reflect now and quickly abandon this thought; it is empty and yields nothing, leading only to needless toil and hardship.
You should now swiftly seek the Two Vehicles, so that you may early escape birth and death.
The Bodhisattva then thought: "This is the speech of Māra, intended to destroy my mind. [He said:
"You should concern yourself only with your own minor affairs; do not, on the contrary, worry about me for the sake of my many concerns."
According to the karma one has created, each receives their respective retribution; one relies upon karma, and karma is one's true friend.
You, too, shall experience retribution according to your karma, relying upon karma, with karma as your kinsman.
Evil Māra Pāpīyān!
Return now quickly along the path you came.
Because you have tormented me, you shall suffer for a long night.
Māra immediately felt ashamed and, concealing his form, departed; this is called the bodhisattva’s adamantine diligence, which Māra cannot destroy.
What is called the bodhisattva’s peerless diligence?

At that time, the diligence practiced by the Bodhisattva surpassed that of hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of other bodhisattvas, beyond the reach of calculation or analogy; how much less could it be matched by other śrāvakas or those training in the two vehicles?
By the power of diligence, one is able to fully embrace all the wholesome dharmas of all Buddhas and abandon every unwholesome dharma without exception; this is called peerless diligence.
"What is called the bodhisattva’s balanced diligence?
It is diligence that is neither excessive nor lax; such diligence is termed balanced diligence."
"What is called the exalted and supreme diligence of a bodhisattva?
It is when a bodhisattva generates the vow of great diligence to cause their present body to possess the physical marks of a Buddha, thinking:
'When I attain Buddhahood, may I have the mark of the invisible crown and a halo extending one fathom.'"
"May I fully attain the Buddha’s marks and signs, unimpeded wisdom, and great sovereignty"—
this is called "exalted and superior diligence.
What is called "the blazing diligence of a bodhisattva"?
For example, just as pure gold and mani-jewels are free from defilement, their radiance is blazing and their forms are exquisitely manifest;
the brilliance of the refined gold is immeasurably incandescent, and the mani-jewel is resplendent and transparently clear.
The diligence of a bodhisattva is likewise thus, free from all defilements.
What are the defilements of diligence?
What are the obscurations of diligence?
Laziness is the defilement of diligence; indolence is the cataract of diligence.
Lack of contentment in eating is the defilement of diligence; craving sleep is the cataract of diligence.
A fondness for socializing is the defilement of diligence; failing to perceive non-self is the obstacle to diligence.
This is called the defilement of diligence and the obstruction of diligence;
to eliminate such defilements and obstructions is called the "blazing diligence" of a bodhisattva. "Good son!
What is meant by the bodhisattva’s constant and perpetual diligence?

It is when one’s movements and deportment never depart from diligence; whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one never ceases or abandons it, and neither body nor mind ever slackens. This is called the bodhisattva’s constant and perpetual diligence.
"What is called the pure diligence of a bodhisattva? It is as follows:
through constant and perpetual diligence, whatever evil or unwholesome karma has arisen—which can obstruct the dharmas of the path and cause decline—is entirely severed and abandoned.

Furthermore, all wholesome dharmas that do not create obstacles for the causes of nirvāṇa, which assist the dharmas of the path and establish one in the state of the path, are all extensively cultivated, increased, and made to blaze forth."
To ensure that even the most subtle evil of a single thought-moment does not arise, let alone great evils—
this is called the pure diligence of a bodhisattva.
What is meant by the diligence of a bodhisattva that is not shared with the two vehicles?

When Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas traverse worlds throughout the ten directions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, filled with the blazing, fierce fires of the Avīci hells, and if there are beings in such worlds beyond who suffer extreme misery, being without refuge or rescue—even if it be but a single sentient being in such distress—the Bodhisattva can endure passing through great fires across immeasurable worlds, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in order to deliver and bring that one suffering being to maturity.
If this is so even for a single being, how much more so for many sentient beings whom one does not rescue?
This is beyond the reach of all non-Buddhists and those training in the two vehicles; it is called the bodhisattva’s diligence that is unique and not shared with the two vehicles.
"What is meant by 'the diligence of a bodhisattva who does not disparage himself'?
A bodhisattva reflects thus:

'The Buddhas of the three periods of time all attained immeasurable virtues through even slight diligence; they were able to accumulate ascetic practices over a long duration and thereby achieve equal and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, I shall now gradually plant the roots of virtue through slight diligence, and before long I too shall undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.'"
This is called the bodhisattva’s diligence of not disparaging oneself.
What is called the bodhisattva’s diligence of non-retrogression?

It is when a bodhisattva does not give rise to a mind of renunciation because their own diligence is slight or because they are poor and lack wealth and treasures; rather, they constantly cultivate diligence directed toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

"All Buddhas of the past, future, and present three periods of time have all attained Bodhi through the accumulation of subtle and refined diligence; I shall not now disparage myself on account of my lowly status."

"By means of subtle diligence, one accumulates all manner of wholesome merits for the sake of all sentient beings to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. One does not enter *nirvāṇa* for one's own pleasure; rather, one would sooner dwell in hell for a long time for the sake of sentient beings. This is called the non-retrogressive diligence of a bodhisattva."
“Good son! Possessing these ten matters is called the bodhisattva’s fulfillment of diligence.
*Ratnamegha Sūtra*, Fascicle One.”
The *Ratnamegha Sūtra*, Scroll II,
translated by the Tripitaka Master Mandaraka of Funan during the Liang Dynasty:
"Good son, there are further ten dharmas possessed by Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas which are called being endowed with the perfection of dhyāna."
Pāramitās. What are the ten? They are:

accumulating great merit; profound revulsion toward all evils; being able to exert diligent effort; possessing extensive learning; having non-perverted understanding; understanding phenomena and inclining toward the Dharma; having sharp faculties and intelligence; possessing a purely wholesome mind; being skilled in the wisdom of meditative concentration; and not being attached to the signs of dhyāna.
"What is meant by 'gathering great merit'? It means having long accumulated roots of goodness within the Mahāyāna;

in every place of birth, one constantly upholds the good precepts and encounters spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra). In life after life, one is always born into families of the Kṣatriya caste, prominent Brahmin lineages, or wealthy householders. In whatever place one is born, one is always born into a family of right view that increases wholesome dharmas. One remembers the skillful means of the practices one has cultivated and does not abandon them, never being separated from spiritual friends, bodhisattvas, and all Buddhas."
Gradually increasing his observation of all phenomena, he reflected:

"The world is great suffering; it is constantly oppressed and tormented by calamities without a moment's respite. It is long subjected to manifold sufferings and blinded by ignorance, all because of craving and desire."
Sensual desire is the root; I should not now associate with sensual desire as ordinary people do.

The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have taught that sensual desire arises from deluded conceptualization, and they have condemned its faults through immeasurable causes and conditions, likening it to piercing a person’s heart and kidneys with a wooden stake.

Desire is like a sharp spear; desire is like the edge of a sword; desire is like a venomous snake; desire is like a blazing flame; desire is like festering pus, which must not be touched or approached.
Desire is like a mass of foam; desire is like a mirage;
desire is like a magical illusion; desire is like a dream. Desire is impure, making one foul and loathsome; desire is like a ripening boil; desire is like putrid, rotting flesh.

Having thus cultivated the perception of revulsion toward desire, he shaved off his hair and beard, abandoned his property and livelihood, left the household life to study the Path, donned the dharma robes, and became a śramaṇa.

"Having gone forth in the True Dharma, with faith in leaving the home life for the homeless state to study the Path, one exerts great diligence so that those who have not yet attained wholesome qualities may attain them, those who have not yet attained wisdom may attain wisdom, and those who have not yet attained realization may attain realization."

"Through such causes and such conditions, by virtue of these matters, one attains great learning (*bahuśruta*); one is able to proclaim both the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), skillfully knowing that the conventional truth is itself the ultimate truth, and skillfully knowing the non-perverted dharmas according to their true nature and characteristics."
“What is the thorough knowledge of the characteristics of phenomena?
It is right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.”
“Having attained the vision of the right path, their faculties become increasingly sharp and superior, and their minds are constantly fixed upon the Way.

Because their faculties are so sharp, they give rise to a profound sense of revulsion; they distance themselves from the clamor and bustle of the great masses, and they remain far removed from thoughts of desire, greed, hatred, and false views, as well as from a malicious intent to harm. They distance themselves from kinsmen, from fame and gain, and from all things pertaining to body and mind.”
"One should constantly and mindfully observe one's own mind to see whether it is dwelling on what is wholesome, unwholesome, or neutral.
If the mind dwells on the wholesome, one should dwell on the superior wholesome.
By dwelling on the superior wholesome, joy arises in the mind, giving rise to faith and delight."
What is this superior wholesome mind?
It is the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
What are these thirty-seven factors?

The four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path—these are called the supreme virtues and are the true limbs of the path.
"If the mind is still unwholesome, one should give rise to the utmost revulsion toward it.
By practicing frequent observation and diligently applying skillful means, one cuts off what is unwholesome.
What is unwholesome? "
Greed, hatred, and delusion.
Greed is of three kinds:
superior, middling, and inferior.
What constitutes superior greed?
When the mind of desire oppresses the body, right view is impaired;
when the mind of desire is slight, one is devoid of shame and remorse.
What is the mind devoid of shame and dread?

If one restrains the body, maintains mental stillness, and dwells alone in the forests and wilds, yet at that time one contemplates sensual thoughts which increase and blaze up, cherishing those sensual thoughts and praising them—because of those sensual thoughts, when performing such contemplation, there is no sense of shame.
What is lack of shame (*āhrīkya*)?

It is, through the influence of desire, the performance of desire, and the conditions of desire, to utter words of resentment toward one's parents, to feel no fear or dread in the presence of those worthy of respect, and furthermore, to lack any sense of shame while falsely representing oneself as possessing virtuous qualities.
Because of this desire, at the time of death one falls into the evil realms; this is called superior desire.
What is called middling desire?
If, after having experienced desire, one gives rise to a sense of weary detachment or a mind of regret, this is called middling desire.
What is called "inferior desire"?

If the thought of desire ceases immediately upon physical contact; or if, though a defiled thought arises during conversation, that thought is extinguished as soon as it is conceived; or if the thought of desire also ceases upon seeing an object of desire—this is called inferior desire.
Regarding desire (*kāma*): all clothing, food and drink, and articles for the maintenance of the body are collectively termed desire.
Hatred (*vyāpāda*) also has three types:
superior, middling, and inferior.
What constitutes the highest form of hatred?

It is when, while causing distress to another, one gives rise to deep-seated anger; or commits one of the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*); or commits each of these five heinous crimes individually; or slanders the True Dharma (*saddharma*), and so forth.

Such offenses are beyond the reach of calculation or analogy; when the body perishes and life ends, one falls into the great hells to undergo punishment. As for the remaining retribution, even if one is born among humans, their skin and body will be black and emaciated, both eyes will be bloodshot, their disposition will be constantly prone to rage, and they will harbor much malice and intent to harm.
For this reason, it is called "superior anger.
What is called "middling anger"?
When one quickly feels remorse for the various evils committed and immediately practices the methods of counteraction, this is called middling anger.
What is called "inferior anger"?

It refers to uttering harsh words, engaging in derision or reproach, accumulating minor unwholesome karma, or occasionally giving rise to anger that is immediately countered; this is termed inferior anger.
“Delusion is also of three kinds:
superior, middling, and inferior.
What is superior delusion?
When one commits evil without remorse, fails to give rise to shame or dread, and feels no sense of weariness toward it, this is called the highest degree of delusion.
What is called the middling degree of delusion?

When one has committed evil with the body, one immediately gives rise to regret; one confesses and repents before fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*) and does not proclaim one's own virtues—this is called the middling degree of delusion.
What is called "inferior delusion"?
It refers to the minor transgressions of those precepts established by the Tathāgata that are not of a grave nature; for this reason, it is called inferior delusion.

When the virtuous mind of a Bodhisattva-mahāsattva arises, he is able to turn back greed, hatred, and delusion; he is able to eliminate craving for desire, eliminate attachment to desire, and eliminate clinging to desire.
By means of a wholesome mind, one causes desire not to arise.
What is called an indeterminate mind?

When this mind arises, it does not take external objects as its object, nor internal objects; it does not take what is wholesome as its object, nor what is unwholesome; it does not proceed from meditative concentration, nor from wisdom.
Just as when one awakens from sleep, the eyes do not see clearly and are neither directed toward the wholesome nor the unwholesome—this is called the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).

When such an indeterminate mind arises, the bodhisattva employs skillful means to exhort himself to give rise to a wholesome mind, causing joy to arise and abiding securely in the wholesome; this is called a bodhisattva attaining a wholesome mind.

By means of a virtuous mind, one contemplates all phenomena as being like an illusion, like a dream, like a mirage in the heat, and like an echo; [one discerns]: "This is a wholesome dharma, this is not a wholesome dharma; this is a vehicle that follows the tracks of the Dharma, this is a vehicle that does not follow the tracks of the Dharma."

“A bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates all phenomena and gives rise to a wholesome mind; taking the Dharma as his object of perception and making the mind his precursor, he should skillfully maintain his mind and harmonize his mind, and skillfully maintain all phenomena and subdue all phenomena.”
Having seen the True Dharma, by virtue of this condition, one attains tranquil concentration (*samādhi*).
Taking the mind as the object, one binds the mind to the mind and gradually enters tranquil concentration; binding the mind to the mind, one dwells correctly in samādhi.
Because the mind is tranquil and concentrated, it is able to be single-minded;
because the mind is single-minded, there is uninterrupted continuity;
and because one has attained a concentrated mind, the mind is constantly serene.
Because the mind is tranquil, joy and happiness arise; thus one eliminates sensual desire, evil, and unwholesome states.
With directed thought and sustained thought, one attains the joy and happiness born of concentration, accomplishing the first dhyāna.
Without directed thought and with diminished sustained thought, one attains the joy and happiness born of concentration, accomplishing the second dhyāna.
With the fading away of joy, one attains the third dhyāna, characterized by equanimity and mindfulness while experiencing bliss;
with the abandoning of both joy and bliss, one dwells in a mind of equanimity and attains the fourth dhyāna;
having removed the view of self, abandoned sorrow and joy, and relinquished both suffering and pleasure, one practices the fourth dhyāna of pure mindfulness and equanimity.
All liberations are free from the marks of form, like empty space; one should contemplate the mental characteristics of sentient beings and the characteristics of empty space as a single liberation.
For this reason, when the marks of form cease, the marks of emptiness arise;
once the marks of affliction and destruction have ceased, the mark of boundless empty space is established.
Following the sign of infinite space, one next contemplates consciousness; because consciousness is infinite, the sign of space ceases.
As the contemplation of consciousness gradually diminishes until only a minimal amount of consciousness remains, it is called the Sphere of Nothingness (ākiṃcanyāyatana).
Furthermore, contemplating whether this consciousness exists or does not exist is called the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana).
The cessation of all perceptions and feelings is called the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Although a bodhisattva enters this absorption of cessation, they do not abandon the teaching and transformation of sentient beings; nor do they take eternal delight in the absorption of cessation as their final tranquility. Without relinquishing the absorption of cessation, they are able to universally cover sentient beings with compassion;
even the arising of the minds of pity (*karuṇā*), joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) within the state of cessation is likewise so.

"At that time, the Bodhisattva attains the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), yet he does not consider the twelve gates of dhyāna or the five supernormal powers to be sufficient for himself; instead, he seeks the supreme Dharma of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, so that his ornaments and merits may be fully perfected."
“Good son! Possessing these ten matters is called a bodhisattva who is endowed with the dhyāna-pāramitā. Good son!”
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva is said to have perfected wisdom. What are these ten? They are: being endowed with the excellence of non-self;

skillfully understanding karmic retribution; skillfully understanding conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); skillfully understanding the uninterrupted continuity of birth and death (*saṃsāra*); skillfully understanding the methods for escaping birth and death; skillfully understanding the two vehicles of the śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha; skillfully understanding the Mahāyāna; skillfully understanding the wisdom that obstructs demonic activities; non-perverted wisdom; and peerless wisdom.

“Good son! What is the excellence of non-self? A bodhisattva observes form, feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness with wisdom. He contemplates that form is unborn, unarisen, and that its cause of arising is not seen; feeling is also unborn, unarisen, and its cause of arising is not seen; perception is also unborn, unarisen, and its cause of arising is not seen; formations are also unborn, unarisen, and their cause of arising is not seen; consciousness is also unborn, unarisen, and its cause of arising is not seen. Even cessation is unborn, unarisen, and its cause of arising is not seen. Furthermore, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is neither seen, nor born, nor arisen.”
