Because the ocean of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is profoundly deep and difficult to traverse, being inconceivable; because it transcends all mental activity and verbal expression; because it is immeasurable and boundless, equal to the realm of empty space; because it surpasses all that is known by non-Buddhists through divination, portents, and incantations; and because his mind is always in accordance with reality, free from all falsehood.

"Furthermore, I have heard that for the sake of sentient beings, the Bodhisattva performs his deeds without giving rise to weariness or aversion, and without experiencing alarm or fear. His willpower is firm and solid; he bears the heavy burden and is able to generate the great aspiration that fulfills all the pāramitās, gradually bringing all the Buddha-dharmas to completion."
His mind is unimpeded, with no one equal to him; he possesses firm diligence, firm adornment, firm wisdom, firm vows, immovable vows, and peerless vows.

Why is this? Because it accords with the characteristics of bodhi; through gradual increase and expansion until fulfillment, one knows it as it truly is, without falsehood, and the mind is free from doubt.
"How can one cultivate faith and remain free from doubt?
One should reflect thus:

'From the first generation of the bodhicitta until sitting at the site of enlightenment, I shall attain unimpeded and unhindered knowledge of all phenomena, understanding them clearly and without obscuration; I shall attain the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, knowledge of past lives, knowledge of the supernormal powers, and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows, such that in a single kṣaṇa I shall fully know the three periods of time.'"

With such wisdom, he observes the realm of sentient beings; he sees that some have unwholesome physical karma, unwholesome verbal karma, and unwholesome mental karma, that they slander the noble ones, and give rise to great false views. He also knows that due to these causes and conditions of false views, at the dissolution of the body after death, they fall into the great hells.

He observes that other sentient beings cultivate wholesome physical karma, cultivate wholesome verbal karma, and cultivate wholesome mental karma; they do not slander the noble ones and are endowed with right view. By these causes and conditions, at the dissolution of the body after death, they are reborn in the heavens.
Thus observing the distinctions between the good and evil of all sentient beings, he forms this thought:
"When I was originally practicing the bodhisattva path, I made a great vow:
'If I myself attain enlightenment, I shall also cause others to attain it.'"
"My vows are fulfilled; my words are true and without falsehood.
Thus, one has no doubt in this matter:
"I have heard that the Tathāgata possesses only the One Vehicle (ekayāna); this is true and not inverted, being without falsehood."
Why is this? It is, for example, like the many small islands in Jambudvīpa; all these small islands depend upon Jambudvīpa for their existence and are likewise called by the same name, "Jambudvīpa.
The Tathāgata’s One Vehicle is also like this: all vehicles emerge from the Great Vehicle. Therefore, the One Vehicle is named the Tathāgata’s Great Vehicle.
Furthermore, one does not give rise to doubt or confusion regarding this, but knows it as it truly is; thus, the bodhisattva has faith in the Tathāgata-yāna.
They have also heard various teachings and various sūtras spoken by the Tathāgata, all of which are without exception true.
Why is this? The Tathāgata, according to the beings he seeks to transform and according to whatever dharma they inquire about, answers them accordingly.
Yet, in this matter, he is able to know it as it truly is, and they accept it with faith and without doubt.
"I have heard that the profound and wondrous voices of the Buddhas are truly real, and my mind has no doubt regarding this matter. Why is this?

If even the devas, having cultivated but a small amount of merit, obtain such profound, wondrous, and gentle voices, how much more so for the Tathāgata, who is fully endowed with immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of merits?"
To have deep faith in this and give rise to no doubt is called a bodhisattva’s faith in the profound and far-reaching voice of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, they believe that the Tathāgata can expound all dharmas with a single sound, such that according to the faculties and dispositions of each being, all doubts are entirely removed, yet every sentient being thinks, "The World-Honored One is speaking to me alone."

The Buddha expounds all dharmas with a single voice, and sentient beings, according to their respective types, each believe and understand them; this is neither through the formation of conceptual thought nor through the absence of conceptual thought, but is known as it truly is, without any falsehood, such that they can give rise to no doubt or perplexity regarding this matter.
“Good son! To be endowed with these ten matters is called a bodhisattva’s profound faith and lack of doubt. Good son!”
Furthermore, there are ten qualities of a bodhisattva that are like the great ocean.

What are these ten? They are: being a great treasury of jewels; being deep and far-reaching, difficult to fathom; being vast and immeasurable; being gradually deeper in successive stages; not dwelling together with afflictions; having the single characteristic of quiescence; receiving and containing all competing streams of water; never missing the time of its tides; being able to serve as a place of refuge for others; and being inexhaustible.
"How is it that a bodhisattva is a great treasure trove?
Just as the great ocean is the source from which all manner of jewels emerge, and though the people of Jambudvīpa all come to compete for them, they cannot cause it to diminish;

so too is the bodhisattva like a treasure trove. Boundless sentient beings all cultivate the bodhisattva practice with faith, yet the treasury of their merit does not diminish. This is called the bodhisattva being like a great treasure trove."
"Just as the great ocean is deep, vast, and difficult to cross;
so too is the Bodhisattva: the ocean of the Dharma of their wisdom cannot be crossed by any demons or non-Buddhists. This is called the Bodhisattva being deep, vast, and difficult to cross."
"Just as the great ocean is vast and boundless, so too is the Bodhisattva;
their merit and wisdom are vast and boundless. This is called the Bodhisattva being like the great ocean—profound, vast, and boundless."

"Just as the great ocean becomes progressively deeper, so too does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva become progressively deeper as they accomplish all-knowledge (sarvajñatā). This is called the Bodhisattva being like the great ocean, becoming progressively deeper."
"It is, for example, like the great ocean, which does not harbor a dead corpse. Why is this?
Because such is the nature of the ocean."
In the Dharma-ocean of a Bodhisattva, all fetters, outflows, the corpses of afflictions, and evil associates do not even share a single night’s lodging.
Why is this? Because it is the natural law of a Bodhisattva.
"Just as when the great ocean is filled by the confluence of all rivers, they all become of one single taste;

so too it is with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva: when pure, white, and virtuous deeds, along with immeasurable and universal merits, reach the ocean of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), they likewise become of one single taste, equal and without distinction."
"Just as the great ocean can contain hundreds of thousands of streams, yet that great ocean neither increases nor decreases;

so too it is with the bodhisattva, who hears and receives all Buddha-dharmas and also analyzes and explains them for the sake of sentient beings, without increase or decrease. This is called the bodhisattva being like the great ocean, neither increasing nor decreasing."
"How is it that, for example, the great ocean does not exceed its limits with the tides?
A bodhisattva is likewise; regarding those sentient beings who are to be brought to maturity, he also does not exceed his limit."
"Just as the great ocean serves as a dwelling place and refuge for all beings with massive bodies, so too is the bodhisattva-mahāsattva likewise;
he acts as a dwelling place and refuge for all beings of great resolve. This is called the bodhisattva being like the great ocean as a dwelling place and refuge."
"Just as the great ocean is inexhaustible, so too is the bodhisattva mahāsattva; for all sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma according to their needs, and this too is inexhaustible."
“Good son! Possessing these ten matters is what defines a bodhisattva as being like the great ocean. Good son!”
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas of a bodhisattva called subtle wisdom.

What are the ten? They are: skillfully knowing the way of transcendence; skillfully knowing the dharmas of transcendence; skillfully knowing that all dharmas are of one and the same characteristic; skillfully knowing that all dharmas have the characteristic of being like an illusion; skillfully knowing the characteristics of all dharmas; skillfully knowing the profound twelve links of dependent origination; skillfully knowing that all karmas are inconceivable; skillfully knowing the meaning of all dharmas; skillfully knowing the meaning of reality as it is; and skillfully knowing the wisdom of reality as it is.
“Good son! What is meant by a bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of the Dharma of the essential way out?
A bodhisattva is able to observe with wisdom that all sentient beings are ablaze with greed and hatred and shrouded in the darkness of ignorance, and reflects as follows:”
"How do sentient beings attain liberation?

By observing that all things are identical in their single characteristic, one knows that all phenomena are like illusory forms; knowing all phenomena as they truly are, one can transcend the profound causes and conditions, know that karma is inconceivable, know that all dharmas are signless while yet discerning the various types of karma, and know dependent origination as well as the characteristics of all karmic actions.
By means of such subtle wisdom, one fully understands the meaning of all the teachings spoken by the Buddhas;
because of this understanding of the meaning, what is seen is reality;
and because of seeing reality, one is then able to deliver sentient beings from birth and death.
"Good son! Possessing these ten matters is called the subtle wisdom of a bodhisattva. Good son!"
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains appropriate eloquence (*yathārtha-pratibhāna*). What are these ten?
The Buddha spoke thus:

"All dharmas are without self, without sentient beings, without life-span, without person, without agent, without knower, and without seer. All dharmas possess such characteristics: all dharmas are empty, all dharmas are illusory and deceptive, lacking a master; all dharmas are conceptual constructions without reality, all arising from causes and conditions."
“Good son! To be endowed with these ten matters is called the bodhisattva’s eloquence of accordance with circumstances. Good son!”
Furthermore, there are ten qualities of a bodhisattva that are called eloquence.

What are these ten? His discourse is without impediment; his speech is inexhaustible; his words are soft and smooth; they are pleasing and infinite; he does not fear the great assembly; his speech is not base or inferior; his speech is free from timidity or dread; his speech has no equal; his words are not loathed by others; and although his speech is immeasurable, it does not deviate from the meaning of the four reliances.
"Noble son!
Being endowed with these ten matters is called the eloquence of a bodhisattva. Noble son!"
Furthermore, there are ten qualities of a bodhisattva that are called "pure eloquence.

What are these ten? His speech is not stammering; his speech is without fear; his speech is not base or inferior; his speech is neither coarse nor arrogant; his meaning is not lowly or trivial; his speech is without deficiency or omission; his voice is clear and penetrating; his voice is without deficiency or omission; his words are timely and free from error; and his eloquence is not harsh or crude.
"What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining eloquence free from stammering?
Because they have no fear of the majesty of the great assembly, their speech is not faltering.
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining eloquence free from terror?"
Because their essential nature is upright, they have nothing to fear.
What is meant by a bodhisattva attaining eloquence that is not base?
For what reason?
A bodhisattva dwells among the great assembly like a lion, without hesitation or fear.
What is meant by "a bodhisattva’s speech is neither coarse nor arrogant"?
For what reason?
Because they have eliminated the fetters and afflictions. Good son!
Because there are afflictions, one's words will necessarily be coarse and haughty.
"What is meant by 'the meaning of a bodhisattva is not base or small'?
For what reason?
Because they have well attained the Dharma; having already deeply understood the Dharma, its meaning is clear to them."
"What is meant by 'the bodhisattva’s speech being free from deficiency'?
For what reason?
Because they have a thorough understanding of all treatises; for if one's understanding of treatises is meager, then their eloquence will be deficient."
"What is meant by 'the Bodhisattva’s voice being without deficiency or shortness'? Why is this?
Because the Bodhisattva fully understands all sounds and voices."
"What is meant by a bodhisattva speaking at the appropriate time?
It means that if one should speak first, one does not become attached to what follows; and if one should speak later, one does not become attached to what preceded it. Why is this?"
Because the bodhisattva skillfully knows the proper time.
What is meant by "the bodhisattva’s eloquence is not coarse or harsh"?
It means that he does not speak to those who would not find it pleasing.
Why is this? Because all verbal transgressions arise from various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); by severing these evils, what is spoken becomes gentle and supple.
A Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva possesses no lack of analytical eloquence (*pratibhāna*).
Why is this? Because the faculties of the bodhisattva have already become entirely sharp. Good son!
Because their faculties are dull and dark, they possess indistinct eloquence;
those with sharp faculties are not so. "Good son!
Possessing these ten matters is called the pure eloquence of a bodhisattva. "Good son,
there are further ten dharmas of a bodhisattva called the eloquence of joyful exposition.
What are the ten? They are:

affectionate speech, speech without frowning, speech that is meaningful, speech that accords with the Dharma, impartial speech, speech that does not exalt oneself, speech that does not disparage others, unadulterated speech, speech that does not provoke irritation, and various forms of eloquence.
“Good son! A bodhisattva’s pleasant speech can cause joy and happiness to arise in the minds of sentient beings;
with a serene and gracious countenance, they bring comfort to all.”
"The Bodhisattva’s analytical eloquence regarding meaning (*arthapratibhāna*) is able to delight the assembly with beautiful speech.
The Bodhisattva’s analytical eloquence regarding the Dharma (*dharmapratibhāna*) provides instruction and benefit.
The Bodhisattva’s analytical eloquence regarding equality (*samatāpratibhāna*) always preaches the Dharma for sentient beings with an impartial mind, enabling all to be completely joyful."
“A bodhisattva does not preach the Dharma out of self-exaltation, for they have eliminated all conceit and the mind that considers oneself right;
a bodhisattva preaches the Dharma through shared activity, for the sake of gladdening sentient beings.”
“A bodhisattva does not disparage others’ preaching of the Dharma, because their mind is able to remain single-mindedly focused.
A bodhisattva is untainted by speech, because they firmly uphold the pure precepts to gladden sentient beings.”
“A bodhisattva does not speak words that cause affliction or provocation, because they delight sentient beings through the power of patience.
A bodhisattva possesses various forms of eloquence, because they delight sentient beings through the power of joyful speech.”
“Good son! Possessing these ten matters is called the bodhisattva’s eloquence of joyful speech. Good son!”
Furthermore, there are ten qualities of a bodhisattva that constitute skillful preaching, enabling sentient beings to believe and accept it.

What are these ten? They are: preaching the Dharma to those who are capable vessels for the Dharma; preaching the Dharma in accordance with their faculties and dispositions; not preaching to those who would revile or disparage; not preaching to followers of external paths or heterodox views; not preaching to those who are arrogant and lack sincerity; not preaching to those who lack faith; not preaching to those who are sycophantic, deceitful, or hypocritical; not preaching to those who seek only a livelihood; not preaching to those who seek gain and offerings, or who are stingy, greedy, or envious; and not preaching to those who are insane, deluded, deaf, or mute.
“Good son! For what reason does a bodhisattva not practice stinginess regarding the Dharma?
He bestows all the dharmas he has attained upon sentient beings, causing them to gain faith and understanding; he does not act as a master who keeps things secret and fails to explain them.”

A bodhisattva never gives rise to a mind lacking compassion toward sentient beings, nor does he exclude them; however, for those who are not fit vessels for the Dharma, he enters into a state of equanimity.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
If these sentient beings are not taught this, for whom else should it be taught?”
The Buddha said:
"To those who possess faith, I shall speak;
to those whose roots of goodness are matured and who are capable vessels of the Dharma, I shall speak."

To those who have planted various roots of goodness under past Buddhas; whose minds are not crooked or deceitful and are free from hypocrisy; who do not feign majestic deportment through illusion or delusion; who do not seek fame for the sake of gain and offerings; who are constantly protected by spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra); who, possessing wisdom, are able to follow with faith and understanding upon hearing [the Dharma]; who have sharp faculties; who, having heard the Dharma, are able to practice it with diligent vigor; and who are able to accord with the Buddha’s teachings—to such sons of good family as these, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas preach the Dharma.
“Good son! Being endowed with these ten matters is called a bodhisattva who is skillfully able to preach the Dharma so that sentient beings believe and accept it. Good son!”
Furthermore, there are ten qualities by which a bodhisattva is called a Dharma-preacher who expounds the Dharma.
What are these ten? They are:
cultivating and accumulating the Buddha-dharmas while being able to expound the Dharma, and yet not perceiving any dharma while being able to cultivate and accumulate them;
He does not perceive any dharma that can sever the fetters for which he preaches the Dharma, nor does he perceive the fetters to be severed;
he does not perceive any dharma of revulsion, dispassion, or cessation, yet he speaks thus:
"Dharmas cannot be subject to revulsion, they cannot be subject to dispassion, and they cannot be subject to the characteristic of cessation."
When preaching the Dharma having attained the fruit of srotāpanna, one does not perceive the mark of a srotāpanna;
when preaching the Dharma having attained the fruit of sakṛdāgāmin, one does not perceive the mark of a sakṛdāgāmin;
when preaching the Dharma having attained the fruit of anāgāmin, one does not perceive the mark of an anāgāmin.
When attaining the fruit of Arhatship and preaching the Dharma, one does not perceive the mark of an Arhat;
when attaining the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood and preaching the Dharma, one does not perceive the mark of a Pratyekabuddha;
when severing attachment to a self and preaching the Dharma, one neither perceives a self nor perceives attachment.
One preaches the Dharma by observing the retribution of karmic fruits, yet does not perceive any marks of karmic fruit and retribution.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva contemplates all provisional designations as not necessarily being established by way of dharmas.
Within names there are no dharmas, and within dharmas there are no names; it is only by means of worldly convention that names are provisionally established and circulated in the world.

Because of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there are provisional names, but when viewed from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they do not exist; they are all entirely false and deceptive, deluding ordinary people.
“Good son! One who possesses these ten matters is called a Bodhisattva Dharma-preacher who expounds the Dharma. Good son!”
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas of a bodhisattva called "firm dharmas. What are these ten?

Although the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva contemplates the reality of form (*rūpa*), he does not destroy the characteristic of form; although he contemplates the reality of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness (*vedanā-saṃjñā-saṃskāra-vijñāna*), he likewise does not destroy the characteristics of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Although the Bodhisattva contemplates the reality of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), he does not destroy the characteristic of the desire realm; although he contemplates the reality of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), he does not destroy the characteristic of the form realm; although he contemplates the reality of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), he does not destroy the characteristic of the formless realm. Although he contemplates the reality of all phenomena (*dharmas*), he does not destroy the characteristics of all phenomena; although he contemplates the reality of all phenomena, he does not destroy the conventional designation of "sentient beings. Although he contemplates the emptiness and stillness of phenomena, he does not ultimately fall into the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*); although he contemplates the reality of all phenomena, he does not destroy the True Path (*samyagmārga*). By means of the wisdom of skillful means (*upāyakauśalyajñāna*), the Bodhisattva thoroughly knows existence and non-existence without grasping at signs (*nimitta*).
"Noble son!
To be endowed with these ten matters is called the Bodhisattva’s firmness in the Dharma. Noble son!"
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva well understands the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
What are these ten? They are: possessing wisdom;

relying on spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); being able to exert diligent effort; remaining far removed from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*); being pure; being respectful; frequently practicing the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*); eliminating attachment to various views; tending toward the Path; and perceiving the true jewel.

"Good son! A bodhisattva possesses wisdom and associates with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra). Upon seeing a spiritual friend, they feel love, respect, and joy; they conceive of the spiritual friend as a World-Honored One (Bhagavān), dwell in reliance upon the spiritual friend, and because of the spiritual friend, they attain diligent vigor. Because of the spiritual friend, they are able to eliminate all unwholesome dharmas."
Although they fulfill all wholesome dharmas, they apply themselves with diligent vigor without weariness, eliminating the hindrances of the aggregates (*skandha-nīvaraṇa*);
because they are free from such obstructions, they diligently cultivate the Path, attaining purity of body, speech, and mental action, and removing all habitual evils;
having attained this purity, they are able to pay respectful homage and offerings.
Because one receives respectful offerings and veneration, one attains the contemplation of emptiness;
by cultivating the contemplation of emptiness, one eliminates all provisional designations;
because all provisional designations are eliminated, one is able to advance toward the Right Path.
"Because one is oriented toward the right path, one is able to see reality.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying,
"World-Honored One!"
"What is called 'seeing reality'?
The Buddha replied,
"That which is seen without falsehood is called reality."
The Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is meant by ‘the ultimate reality’?”
The Buddha replied again:
"The non-false and non-delusory dharma is called 'the real'.
The Bodhisattva Apāyajaha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
What is meant by ‘not false’?
The Buddha then replied:
“That which is according to reality and not otherwise is called non-falsehood.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"What is meant by 'according to reality'?
The Buddha replied, "This Dharma can only be known by the mind;
it is difficult to express with words and cannot be fully explained through written characters."
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that the characteristics of dharmas are free from words and letters?”

"It transcends the path of language and exceeds all spheres of mental activity; it is free from all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), without creation or action, and without this or that. It cannot be reached by calculation or deliberation, nor is it a characteristic mark; it surpasses all that is seen by the ignorant and foolish, exceeds the realm of Māra, transcends all abodes of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), and goes beyond the manifestations of mind, thought, and consciousness. It does not abide in the state of cessation (*śānti*) where the noble ones dwell, yet it is that which is realized and known by those noble ones."
“Good son! To be endowed with these ten matters is what is called ‘ultimate suchness. It is the inconceivable realm and the non-dual realm taught by the Omniscient One.”
The Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is this mark of reality (yathābhūtalakṣaṇa) realized?”
"How do you see it?
The Buddha told him: "Good son!
"Only supramundane wisdom can realize and see this Dharma attained by oneself.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

The essential nature of this dharma is ultimately pure; it is not a defiled dharma, but a serene and tranquil dharma, a subtle and most excellent dharma, eternally abiding and immovable, and not a dharma subject to decay.
Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, the nature of phenomena remains ever thus.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas diligently practice difficult and arduous austerities—hundreds of thousands of myriads of kotis of such difficult and arduous austerities—in order to attain this Dharma and establish sentient beings within it.
The Bodhisattva Nivāraṇaviṣkambhin again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Regarding such names as these, are they realized through the body by means of hearing with the wisdom of hearing and reflecting with the wisdom of reflection?”
The Buddha said,
“Good son, it is not so.”
"Why is this? Because by observing the dharmas as they truly are with wisdom, one attains realization through the body.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is it not through the wisdom of hearing that one hears, nor through the wisdom of reflection that one reflects, but rather through the body that one attains realization?
The Buddha said:
“Good son! No. It is not by means of the wisdoms of hearing and reflection that the body can attain realization.”
"Good son! Listen attentively now; I shall speak a parable for you, good son!"

It is like this: at the end of spring, during the height of the heat, in a vast wilderness, there is a person coming from the east wishing to go west, and another person coming from the west wishing to pass toward the east.
The one coming from the west, oppressed by the heat, says to that person:
"I am now oppressed by the heat and am extremely parched with thirst; show me the way—where might there be a cool pond or spring where I may quench my thirst?"
The man coming from the east, who was well-acquainted with the path and skilled in the characteristics of the road, replied to him:
"On the way there is excellent, clear, cool, and beautiful water, free from all saltiness and bitterness; having bathed and drunk my fill there, I have been able to arrive here."
"Good son!
If you wish to proceed there, the paths are many.
Not far from here, there are two roads."
"First is the left-hand path, and second is the right-hand path.
You should now proceed by way of the right-hand path and abandon the left-hand path.

Not far from here, you will see a dense and lush grove that is cool and refreshing; within this grove are many excellent ponds and springs with delicious flowing waters, where you may bathe and drink to dispel your thirst."
The Buddha said: "Good son!
When that thirsty person hears of water and contemplates it, does he become quenched of his thirst upon merely thinking of it?"
The Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying: “No,
World-Honored One!”
"Although we have heard of the Cool Grove, our bodies have not yet realized it through direct experience.
The Buddha said,
"Good sons!..."
This is also like that: one cannot realize the Dharma of true reality merely through the wisdoms of hearing and reflection.
The vast wilderness is like birth and death;
the thirsty and exhausted person is the ordinary worldling bound by fetters, who, oppressed by the heat of afflictions, gives rise to the thirst of craving.
One who well knows the path is like a bodhisattva who well knows the path to all-knowledge;
one who is able to drink the water is like one who has well attained the flavor of the Dharma;
bathing in coolness is like bodily realization.
It is clear, pure, and free from all saltiness or bitterness, just like the true Dharma.
Good son, listen well now; I shall speak another parable for you.

Suppose the Tathāgata were to dwell in Jambudvīpa for the duration of a kalpa, and while his life lasted that long, he were to describe the fragrance of the *sūda* flavor as supremely wonderful, sweet, and pure, praising how it brings joy at the time of eating and how its taste is beyond compare.
"Suppose there were a person who, although they had seen its color, had not yet eaten it; would they have already obtained its taste?
Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin replied to the Buddha, "No, World-Honored One."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha said, “Good son!”
I shall now provide you with another analogy.

Suppose there is a person who has once eaten a delicious fruit; before someone who has not yet obtained it, he praises that fruit as being endowed with perfect color, fragrance, and flavor. When that other person hears this description of the fruit, do they already know its color, fragrance, and flavor?
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying: “No,
World-Honored One!”
The Buddha said, “Good son!
Ordinary people and foolish persons are likewise; they cannot realize and know the true nature of phenomena through the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection alone.”
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
For my sake, you have now skillfully expounded this parable; whoever hears it shall before long likewise obtain the benefit of the Dharma.”
"Why is this? Because if one hears this Dharma, one will certainly realize the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika) and shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha then replied:
"As you have said, those who hear this Dharma will certainly realize the stage of *avaivartika* and shall attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
O son of good family!"
One who possesses these ten matters is called a bodhisattva who well knows the dharma-realm. "Good son,
there are further ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva is said to dwell well in the sphere of emptiness."

What are these ten? They are: skillfully knowing the emptiness of the powers; skillfully knowing the emptiness of the fearlessnesses; skillfully knowing the emptiness of the unique qualities; skillfully knowing the emptiness of the aggregate of ethical discipline; skillfully knowing the emptiness of the aggregate of meditative concentration; skillfully knowing the emptiness of the aggregate of wisdom; skillfully knowing the emptiness of the aggregate of liberation; skillfully knowing the emptiness of the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation; skillfully knowing the emptiness of emptiness; and skillfully knowing the emptiness of the ultimate truths.

Although they know emptiness, they do not grasp at the mark of emptiness, do not form a view of emptiness, and do not rely upon emptiness; nor do they fall into the view of annihilation because of this emptiness, its causes and conditions, or its characteristics.
"Good son! One who possesses these ten matters is said to be a bodhisattva who dwells well in the state of emptiness. Good son!"
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva is said to dwell in the signless (*animitta*).

What are these ten? They are: the removal of external signs; the removal of internal signs; the removal of signs of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); the removal of all signs of clinging to existence; the removal of all signs of objective spheres (*viṣaya*); the removal of all signs of movement and activity; the removal of all signs of destinations and locations; the removal of all signs of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*); the removal of all signs of consciousness (*vijñāna*); and the removal of all signs of the objects of consciousness.
The Bodhisattva Nīvaranaviskambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
If bodhisattvas are already able to abide thus in the signless (*animitta*), how then does the Buddha abide in the signless?"
The Buddha then replied:
"The realm of the Tathāgata is inconceivable. Why is this?
This is because it is not an object of intellectual deliberation.
Should one attempt to deliberate upon it, the mind would become deranged.
Even if all sentient beings were to measure it together, they could not know the matters of this shore and the other shore of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? The realm of the Tathāgata is profound and far-reaching, inconceivable.

Like empty space, it transcends all measures and calculations; for those who perceive it with attachment, their minds are constantly inverted, and thus it cannot be conceived or calculated by means of arithmetic.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
I wish to pose a question; I only pray that you will grant me your permission.”
“Good son! Ask whatever you wish; I shall now analyze and explain it for you, and all the Buddhas will likewise grant their approval.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
To be attached to what belongs to the self is not the way of the wise.
World-Honored One, as the Great Lord of the Dharma, how could you possibly engage in self-praise?”
The Buddha said,
“Excellent, excellent!
O son of good family!”
"Listen attentively, listen attentively; I shall explain it for you.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying, "So be it."
“World-Honored One!

The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not praise themselves out of arrogance; they do not do so for the sake of gain or offerings, nor for fame, nor to cause others to know them, nor do they falsely claim for themselves, nor are they sycophantic, crooked, or deceitful.”
Why is this? It is solely for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, so that they may attain peace and happiness and practice the Dharma. Why is this?
I desire to cause sentient beings to give rise to profound faith and reverence toward the Tathāgata;

for those whose minds are filled with great joy and who are capable of being vessels for the Dharma, I wish to ensure their peace and security throughout the long night, that they may obtain wholesome benefits, constantly experience happiness, and even attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Do sentient beings not know that the Tathāgata is the Honored One among devas and the Sovereign Dharma King?”
The Buddha said,
“Good son, I do not know.”

Why is this? Because inferior sentient beings engage in base and defiled karmic actions; possessing little wisdom and little faith, they are constantly possessed by unwholesome states and various evils, and thus do not know that the Tathāgata possesses great majestic power and virtue.
For these reasons, the Tathāgata proclaims his own true virtues so that those sentient beings may believe, accept, and practice them. Good son!

It is like a physician who is well-versed in medical methods; though he dwells in a place where many suffer from illness and pain, there are no other physicians capable of providing treatment, yet these people do not recognize that this physician possesses great majestic power.
At that time, the skilled physician observed that the patients did not recognize the proper prescriptions and medicines, nor did they know what foods they should not eat.
Thereupon, the skilled physician gave rise to great compassion, thinking:
"I shall treat them and eliminate their suffering from illness."
At that time, the skilled physician, in the presence of the multitude, praised his own virtues, saying:
"I am well-acquainted with this illness and well-acquainted with its cause; I am well-acquainted with medicines and their applications, and I shall prescribe them according to what is appropriate."
At that time, the sentient beings conceived faith and reverence toward the skilled physician; because of their faith, they immediately relied upon him.
Then, the skilled physician administered various kinds of medicines according to their needs, and once the people had taken them, their illnesses were entirely cured.
“Good son! At that time, did that physician praise himself?
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"No, World-Honored One.
The Buddha said:

“Good son! The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is like a great king of physicians; he can cure the diseases of affliction of sentient beings, and he also knows the causes and origins from which those afflictions arise, bestowing upon them the universal medicine of the Great Dharma.”
Sentient beings are ignorant and shrouded by afflictions, so they do not know that the Tathāgata is the Great King of Physicians;
yet the Tathāgata constantly speaks of himself before the masses in various places, and at such times, sentient beings give rise to faith and reverence, taking refuge in the Tathāgata.
The Holy Lord, the World-Honored One, is like a king of physicians; by means of the great medicine of the Dharma, he is able to extinguish the diseases of affliction of sentient beings.
What is meant by this "great medicine of the Dharma"?
Those with greed are treated with the contemplation of impurity; those with hatred are treated with loving-kindness; those with delusion are treated with the Dharma of dependent origination.
Through such immeasurable medicinal Dharmas, all the diseases of the afflictions can be effectively countered.
"Good son!
It is because the Tathāgata perceives such immeasurable benefits that he praises himself.
Good son!"
One who possesses these ten matters is called a bodhisattva dwelling in the signless (*animitta*).
"Good son, there are further ten dharmas for a bodhisattva that are called the wishless (*apraṇihita*)."
What are the ten? Although one practices generosity, one does not harbor aspirations based on that generosity;
although one maintains the precepts, one likewise does not harbor aspirations based on those precepts.
It is the same for patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom:

although they rely upon the triple world, one does not seek after the characteristics of the triple world; although one seeks awakening, one does not grasp at the characteristics of awakening; although one practices the right path, one does not grasp at the characteristics of the right path; and although one seeks nirvana, one does not grasp at the characteristics of nirvana.

Why is this? Because a bodhisattva has departed from all marks of seeking and aspiration; although they practice all Buddha-dharmas, their mind is always free from any seeking or aspiration. Good son!
Possessing these ten matters is called the bodhisattva’s wishlessness.
"Good son, there are further ten dharmas of the bodhisattva that are called the cultivation of immeasurable loving-kindness."

What are these ten? They are: practicing a compassion that does not depend on location; practicing a compassion that does not follow partiality toward kin; constantly practicing the compassion of the Dharma; cultivating compassion based on meditative concentration; practicing compassion not for the sake of merely abandoning anger; constantly giving rise to compassion for the benefit of all sentient beings; constantly cultivating impartial compassion for sentient beings; practicing compassion not for the sake of merely abandoning affliction and harm; universally cultivating compassion throughout the ten directions; and cultivating supramundane compassion. To possess these ten matters is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation of immeasurable loving-kindness.
“Good son! Furthermore, there are ten dharmas of a bodhisattva called the immeasurable of compassion (*karuṇā-apramāṇa*). What are these ten?

Seeing sentient beings without refuge, without rescue, without protection, and tormented by suffering, the Bodhisattva immediately gives rise to the bodhicitta. Having attained the practice in accordance with the Dharma and having acquired the Dharma, they benefit sentient beings: to those who are greedy, they teach generosity; to those who violate the precepts, they teach the observance of ethical discipline; to those who cause harm, they teach patience; to those who are indolent, they teach diligence; to those with distracted minds, they teach meditative concentration; and to those who are ignorant, they teach wisdom.
Even if they see stubborn and evil sentient beings who do not accept their teachings, the Bodhisattva’s mind does not falter or retreat.
Although they undergo various sufferings for the sake of sentient beings over a long period, their resolve is determined to save them, without ever becoming weary or disheartened.
"Good son! To be endowed with these ten matters is called a bodhisattva’s cultivation of immeasurable compassion. Good son!"
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas of a bodhisattva called the immeasurable joy. What are these ten?
Seeing all sentient beings burning within birth and death, they feel great joy upon attaining liberation from the deceptive master of the three realms of existence.
They give rise to a heart of joy at severing the cords of birth-and-death, trembling, coming-and-going, and karmic fetters;

they give rise to a heart of joy at seeing that within the ocean of birth-and-death, the demons of evil thoughts and the rakshasas of the waters have now been extinguished, and they have escaped such manifold perils of the great ocean of birth-and-death;
they give rise to a heart of joy at toppling the banners of Māra.
With the vajra of wisdom, he shatters the mountain of fetters and afflictions until they are reduced to dust, giving rise to a heart of joy;
thinking, "I have now attained rest for myself and shall cause others to attain rest," he gives rise to a heart of joy;

thinking, "I have now awakened my mind from the state of long slumber within birth and death, and I shall likewise cause all sentient beings—who are bound by craving and blinded by ignorance—to fully awaken," he gives rise to a heart of joy.

I have now attained liberation for myself, having departed from all evil destinies and perilous places; I shall likewise deliver those who have fallen into evil destinies and perilous places—thus I give rise to a heart of joy.

In the wilderness of birth and death, upon the treacherous paths of the six realms of existence, I wandered alone without a companion, circling back and forth, not knowing the right path and ignorant of the directions; I have now found the true path and recognized the directions—thus I give rise to a heart of joy.
I have now drawn near to the city of omniscience and sit beside the seat of the Buddha—thus I give rise to a heart of joy.
"Noble son!
To be endowed with these ten matters is called the bodhisattva’s immeasurable mind of joy. Noble son!"
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas of a bodhisattva called the immeasurable equanimity. What are the ten?
Seeing beautiful forms with the eyes, one enters the state of equanimity without attachment or clinging.

When the ear hears sounds, the nose smells odors, the tongue tastes flavors, the body touches what is smooth and fine, and the mind cognizes phenomena—regarding these five objects of the senses (*pañca-viṣaya*), one does not grasp at their characteristics nor is one afflicted or oppressed, but constantly practices equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Regarding the three types of suffering—the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*)—the mind neither increases nor decreases in response to these three feelings (*vedanā*), remaining unafflicted and unoppressed, and constantly practicing equanimity.
Having accomplished what was to be done and exhausted all fetters of existence (*bhava-saṃyojana*), one constantly practices equanimity.
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:
"I wish to deliver them.
Having already delivered himself, he constantly practices the mind of equanimity.
“Good son! Possessing these ten matters is called the bodhisattva’s immeasurable mind of equanimity. Good son!”
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas of a bodhisattva called the "play of supernatural powers.

What are these ten? They are: manifesting the relinquishing of life; manifesting the taking of birth; manifesting various kinds of youthful play and laughter; manifesting the act of leaving the household life; manifesting the practice of asceticism; manifesting the approach to the tree of enlightenment; manifesting the subduing of Māra and his host of adversaries; manifesting delight in tranquility; manifesting the turning of the wheel of Dharma; and manifesting entry into parinirvāṇa.
The Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by what causes and conditions do you manifest the relinquishing of your lifespan in the Tuṣita Heaven, and so forth, up to manifesting entry into parinirvāṇa?”
The Buddha replied:
“In the Tuṣita Heaven, beings are attached to the five desires and frequently give rise to the perception of permanence;

yet the Bodhisattva is the most supreme and excellent among all sentient beings, remaining unstained by the five desires even as his body passes away. He is able to destroy the sickness of the perception of permanence in sentient beings, causing them to attain the perception of impermanence, so that their minds do not become negligent.”

In the Tuṣita Heaven, there is much negligence; beings do not give rise to a mind of reverence, faith, or delight, but are stained by and attached to sensual desires, do not receive the True Dharma, and take pleasure in play and self-indulgent entertainment throughout the long night. For this reason, the Bodhisattva manifests the relinquishing of his life-span in order to eliminate their negligent minds.
At that time, when sentient beings saw the Bodhisattva relinquish his life, they all abandoned their negligence and gave rise to a mind of weary detachment;
because they abandoned negligence, they immediately resolved to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
“The Bodhisattva manifests various extraordinary signs while dwelling in his mother’s womb, causing sentient beings to believe in and accept his transformation;
though dwelling in the womb, he preaches the Dharma for the multitude, so that they all attain the stage of non-retrogression and swiftly advance toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

“If there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness ripen upon seeing the Bodhisattva as an infant, the Bodhisattva manifests the state of an infant for the sake of maturing the roots of goodness of those beings;
if there are sentient beings whose roots of goodness increase upon seeing the Bodhisattva renounce the household life, the Bodhisattva then leaves home and renounces the world for their sake;
if there are sentient beings whose minds are attached to coarse and debased things, the Bodhisattva manifests the practice of asceticism to bring them to maturity.”

Regarding devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and gandharvas who should be brought to maturity by seeing ascetic practices, he manifests them accordingly to bring them to maturity, and likewise to subdue various non-Buddhists and others.
"Immeasurable sentient beings have long harbored the aspiration:
'When the Bodhisattva swiftly proceeds to the Bodhi tree, I shall follow him.

At that time, the Bodhisattva immediately manifests his approach to the foot of the Bodhi tree; thereupon, these sentient beings attain the stage of non-retrogression (avaivartika) and even give rise to the mind of unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta)."

Furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings who are arrogant, conceited, and self-reliant on their own power, the Bodhisattva—desiring to shatter that mind of arrogance—manifests sitting at the site of enlightenment to subdue the demonic adversaries, causing them to believe and submit.
“The Bodhisattva manifests sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) for the sake of increasing the roots of goodness of sentient beings who delight in tranquility.

When the Bodhisattva sits at the site of enlightenment, he causes all sounds throughout the trichiliocosm to completely disappear, and the trichiliocosm immediately becomes tranquil. This causes those who delight in tranquility to conceive a sense of wonder, leading them all to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and enabling all sentient beings to attain tranquility.”

Furthermore, there are sentient beings who claim to be great teachers and conceive themselves as omniscient, yet they do not know the path of deliverance, do not recognize the supramundane Dharma, and are unaware of the retributions of the present life and future lives; it is for the purpose of subduing such beings that [the Buddha] acts.

"Seeing those who are capable vessels and beings ready for maturation, for their sake, he manifested the attainment of the path of unsurpassed *samyak-saṃbodhi* and proceeded to Vārāṇasī to turn the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Noble Truths three times."
Furthermore, there are sentient beings who are to be matured by the manifestation of entering *nirvāṇa*; for the sake of maturing those beings, [the Bodhisattva] manifests entry into *nirvāṇa*.
It is through such conditions and such purposes that the Bodhisattva manifests sitting at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) and even manifests entry into *nirvāṇa*.
“Good son! Possessing these ten matters is called the bodhisattva’s sporting in supernormal powers. Good son!”
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas of a bodhisattva that are called "being free from the eight difficulties.

What are these ten? They are: being free from evil karma and unwholesome states; never violating the prohibitions and precepts established by the Tathāgata; eliminating greed and envy; having planted various roots of goodness under past Buddhas; constantly cultivating meritorious deeds; being fully endowed with wisdom; skillfully knowing expedient means; skillfully knowing how to make vows; having a mind of great world-weariness; and being able to exert diligent effort.

"A bodhisattva does not enter hell by committing evil karma; though dwelling in hell, they ultimately do not undergo the retribution of hellish suffering, nor can anything they dislike cause them distress.
Although they fall into hell, they do not remain there for long, nor do they give rise to thoughts of malice or harm."
"The bodhisattva’s disposition is disciplined and supple, and they constantly cultivate the ten wholesome paths of action. Because of these ten wholesome paths, they do not fall into the hells.
The bodhisattva does not violate the Buddha's precepts and thus does not fall among animals; though appearing as an animal, they do not undergo the sufferings of an animal.
The bodhisattva does not give rise to greed or envy and thus does not fall among hungry ghosts; though appearing as a hungry ghost, they do not undergo the sufferings of a hungry ghost."
“A bodhisattva never takes birth in a family of wrong views; even if born in a place of wrong views, they will inevitably encounter virtuous friends. Why is this?

Because they have cultivated various virtues in the past, and because they have long planted roots of goodness under past Buddhas, they are always born into families of right view and possess auspicious causes and conditions.”
Because they possess wholesome causes and conditions, their merit increases and expands.
"A bodhisattva never has impaired or deficient faculties; one who lacks such faculties is not a fit vessel for the Dharma."

The Bodhisattva has accumulated merit over a vast period of time and cultivated blessings without weariness. He has cultivated merit everywhere—before various images, stupas, monasteries, and within the Dharma and the Sangha—with a mind that is never indolent. Because he cultivates constantly, his faculties are fully developed and without deficiency, making him a fit vessel for the Dharma.

“A bodhisattva shall never be born in borderlands, among the foolish, the mute, or in other such evil places; like a white sheep, they would be dull-witted and lacking in wisdom, unable to discern the meaning and intent of good and evil, unfit to be a vessel for the Dharma, and likewise ignorant of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.”

The Bodhisattva is born in a central land; he is intelligent, possesses sharp faculties, and has great wisdom and insight. Furthermore, his mind is full of faith and delight, and he associates with those who possess wisdom. He is well able to distinguish between good and evil, is a fit vessel for the Dharma, and has deep faith in śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
Why is this? Because a bodhisattva fundamentally cultivates the power of wisdom.
A bodhisattva is not reborn in the long-lived heavens.

If one were born in the long-lived heavens, one would not behold the appearance of a Buddha in the world, would remain far removed from the fruits of the Path, and would be unable to bring sentient beings to maturity;

for this reason, a Bodhisattva is born in the realm of desire so that, at the time a Buddha appears in the world, they will inevitably encounter the opportunity to transform and guide sentient beings.

“By what causes and conditions, and through what skillful means, does a bodhisattva never take birth in a world where no Buddha resides, nor in a place where the Dharma is not heard, nor even in a place where there is no Saṃgha to whom one may offer support?”
Wherever a bodhisattva is born, they will inevitably encounter the Three Jewels.
Why is this? It is because of the power of their original vow.
Wherever a bodhisattva is born, they will necessarily feel revulsion; their mind will not be arrogant or conceited.

If they hear of the eight difficult conditions or places of evil, they will certainly give rise to weary detachment and find no joy in them, but will diligently cultivate vigor, perfect all wholesome dharmas, and eliminate unwholesome dharmas.
“Good son! One who possesses these ten things is called a bodhisattva who is free from the eight difficulties.
*Ratnamegha Sūtra*, Fascicle Three.”
The Ratnamegha Sūtra, Scroll Four.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Mandarasa from Funan during the Liang Dynasty.
"Good son, there are further ten dharmas of the bodhisattva mahāsattva called 'not forgetting.'"
The Bodhicitta. What are the ten? The mind is free from flattery and deceit, as well as illusion and delusion;

the mind is always auspicious, substantial, clear, pure, and white; one never gives rise to doubt regarding the Buddha, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha; one does not give rise to doubt regarding those who receive and uphold the Buddha-Dharma; one does not harbor thoughts of a teacher while being stingy with the Dharma; one eliminates the stinginess regarding the Dharma and never creates conditions for the extinction of the Buddha-Dharma; one’s words and deeds correspond, and one never falsely receives and upholds the Mahāyāna; if one sees someone receiving and upholding it, one is always able to show them respect; one gradually enters deeply into the Mahāyāna; and one conceives the thought of the Buddha and the thought of a virtuous friend toward those who preach the Dharma.
“Good son!
One who possesses these ten matters is called a bodhisattva who never forgets the mind of enlightenment. Good son!”
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva can recognize past lives.

What are these ten? They are: having extensively revered and made offerings to the Buddhas; upholding the teachings of all Buddhas; being able to purely maintain the precepts; eliminating all doubt and regret; removing all hindrances and obstacles; possessing a mind of great joy; delighting in meditative concentration; constantly receiving birth through transformation; and attaining non-delusive cognition.

Those who make offerings to the Buddha always give rise to reverence for the True Dharma; those who receive and uphold the True Dharma likewise always show reverence. By these causes and conditions, they are able to receive and uphold the Dharma—reciting it, copying it, and explaining it extensively for others—sparing neither body nor life solely for the sake of the True Dharma.
They purely cultivate the practice of the precepts, such that the actions of their body, speech, and mind are all entirely pure.
Because their precepts are pure, their minds are free from doubt or regret.
Because one purely maintains the precepts, there are no hindrances or obstructions;
because there are no hindrances or obstructions, the mind attains joy;
because the mind is joyful, one is able to cultivate meditative concentration.
Because one attains the cultivation of meditative concentration, the place of birth is pure;
because the place of birth is pure, one then attains transformational birth;
because one attains transformational birth, one attains non-delusive consciousness.
Because one attains non-delusive consciousness, one immediately attains the knowledge of past lives;
because one attains the knowledge of past lives, one is able to know one lifetime, two lifetimes, and even up to hundreds of thousands of lifetimes.
"Noble son!
Possessing these ten matters is called a bodhisattva attaining the knowledge of past lives. Noble son!"
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva does not become separated from a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

What are these ten? They are: not being separated from encountering the Buddha, hearing of the Buddha, or recollecting the Buddha; not being separated from constantly hearing the Dharma; not being separated from constantly making offerings to the Saṃgha; not being separated from prostrating to, inquiring after the welfare of, reverencing, joining the palms in homage, and making offerings to all Buddhas and bodhisattvas; not being separated from meeting those of great learning who preach the Dharma; not being separated from hearing about the various *pāramitās*; not being separated from hearing about the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) and the factors of awakening (*bodhyaṅga*); not being separated from hearing about the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*); not being separated from hearing about the four divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*); and not being separated from hearing about the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
“Good son! Possessing these ten matters is called a bodhisattva who does not depart from spiritual friends. Good son!”

Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains distance from evil associates (*pāpamitra*). What are these ten? They are: distancing oneself from evil associates who violate the precepts;

distancing oneself from those who destroy right view; distancing oneself from those who ruin dignified conduct (*īryāpatha*); distancing oneself from those who follow wrong livelihood (*mithyājīva*); distancing oneself from those who delight in worldly talk and frequent noisy crowds; distancing oneself from those who are excessively indolent; distancing oneself from those who take pleasure in and are attached to birth and death (*saṃsāra*); distancing oneself from those who turn their backs on enlightenment (*bodhi*); distancing oneself from the assembly of householders; and distancing oneself from all fetters and afflictions (*saṃyojana-kleśa*).
Although a bodhisattva delights in distancing themselves from such matters, they never give rise to thoughts of affliction or harm, nor do they harbor a mind of contempt or disparagement.
The bodhisattva reflects thus:
"I have heard the Buddha say that the dispositions and desires of sentient beings become defiled through mutual attachment; because of such intimacy, much is ruined."
"Therefore, I should distance myself from all such things. Noble son,
being endowed with these ten matters is called a bodhisattva’s distancing himself from evil associates.
“Good son! Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva attains the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.
What are these ten?

The body of equality, the non-dual body, the pure and inexhaustible body, the body of long-cultivated virtue, the dharma-body, the body of profound depth beyond calculation or measurement, the inconceivable body, the body of quiescent extinction, the space-like body, and the wisdom-body.
“Good son! One who possesses these ten things is called a bodhisattva who has attained the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata.
The Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
When will a bodhisattva attain the fulfillment of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body?
He replied:
“Good son! A bodhisattva of the first stage attains an equal body. Why is this?
The Bodhisattva of the first stage eliminates all evil bodies and becomes equal to all other Bodhisattvas; this is called the "equal body.
The Bodhisattva of the second stage attains a pure body because of the purity of their observance of the precepts.
The Bodhisattva of the third stage attains an inexhaustible body because they have eliminated anger, affliction, and harm.
Bodhisattvas of the fourth stage attain a body that has long accumulated all virtues, because they have cultivated and gathered all Buddha-dharmas;
Bodhisattvas of the fifth stage attain the Dharma-body, because through the power of meditative concentration they know all Buddha-dharmas;
Bodhisattvas of the sixth stage attain a body that cannot be known by worldly calculation or measurement, because it is profound and far-reaching.
Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage attain the inconceivable body by virtue of skillful means;
Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage attain the body of quiescence because they have well eliminated frivolous play and exhausted all afflictions;
Bodhisattvas of the ninth stage attain the space-like body because they attain an unimpeded body that pervades all of space.
A Bodhisattva of the tenth stage attains the body of wondrous wisdom.
Why is this? Because they have thoroughly known all the dharmas of the various stages of the Bodhisattvas.
The Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Is there no distinction between the Dharma-body of a bodhisattva and the Dharma-body of a Tathāgata?”
The Buddha said:
"There is no difference in their bodies; it is only that their merits differ.
Bodhisattva Apāyajaha addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Why is it that while the bodies are without distinction, their merits differ?
The Buddha said:
"The body and the name are not different.
Why is this? Because the body and speech share a single characteristic, yet the characteristics of their respective merits each have their own distinctions."
“What is the mark of perceiving distinct virtues within the body?
The Buddha said, “Good son!
I shall now speak a parable for you to explain this meaning.

For example, all mani-jewels are equally called "mani"; though the name of these jewels is one and the same, those that have been polished and refined shine with brilliance, bringing joy to the mind, like the body of a Tathāgata;
whereas those not polished or refined are like the bodies of Bodhisattvas.

The maṇi-jewel of the Tathāgata’s body and the maṇi-jewel of the Bodhisattva’s body are, in reality, no different; yet the radiance and physical characteristics of the Tathāgata’s maṇi-jewel and the Bodhisattva’s maṇi-jewel are each distinct.
Why is this? The mani-jewel of the Tathāgata’s body is immeasurable, filling the realm of sentient beings and filling the realm of empty space, pure and free from all dust and defilement;
the mani-jewel of the Bodhisattva’s body is limited and cannot fill the realm of empty space.
Why is this? Because there are defilements and hindrances. "Good son!

For example, when the moon reaches the fifteenth day, it is called the "full moon"; the subsequent fifteen days are also called "moon," and even until the end of the month they are all called "moon. Although the name "moon" is the same, its brightness is not like that of the fifteenth-day moon; yet such is the inherent nature of the moon.

The body of the Tathāgata and the body of the Bodhisattva are both called "moon. Just as their names are identical and their reality is likewise identical, so too do their radiant illumination differ between the Bodhisattva and the Tathāgata.

The radiance of a bodhisattva’s body, though brilliantly illuminating, does not equal that of the Tathāgata, whose light is so blazing and intense that it is like the incomparability between the moon at the end of the month and the moon at the beginning of the month.
"Good son! For this reason, although the body of the Tathāgata and the body of the bodhisattva are identical in nature, their merits differ. Good son!"
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas of a bodhisattva called the indestructible vajra body. What are these ten? They are: it cannot be destroyed by desire, hatred, or delusion;

it cannot be destroyed by affliction, harm, pride, attachment to self, self-conceit, or inverted views; it cannot be destroyed by the eight worldly dharmas; it cannot be destroyed by the evil realms; it cannot be destroyed by any suffering; it cannot be destroyed by birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, pain, or distress; it cannot be destroyed by any heterodox paths or divergent views; it cannot be destroyed by any māras, devas, or the retinues of māras; it cannot be destroyed by any śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas; and it cannot be destroyed by the entire realm of desire.
"Good son! One who possesses these ten things is said to have the indestructible vajra body of a bodhisattva. Good son!"
Furthermore, there are ten qualities of a bodhisattva that constitute being a great caravan leader.

What are these ten? They are: being able to cause merchants to follow their instructions; being able to cause merchants to offer them support and respect; being able to act as a guide who does not fear any hardships; being able to serve as a place of reliance for the multitude; being able to provide a basis for others to depend upon; always ensuring they obtain their livelihood; possessing abundant provisions; possessing many rare treasures; having a mind that never knows satiety; and always acting as a vanguard leading them to the great city of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*).
“Good son! How is it that a bodhisattva can cause merchants to follow his instructions?
It is like a caravan leader who skillfully guides a multitude of merchants; whatever he says, they all follow accordingly.”
The Bodhisattva is likewise; skillfully transforming sentient beings, he is able to cause them all to follow him.
Just as a merchant leader is reverently honored and supported by his fellow merchants, so too is the Bodhisattva merchant leader:
those in training and those beyond training, as well as devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, humans, non-humans, and others, all come to reverently honor and support him.
"Just as a caravan leader, being skilled in traversing wildernesses and regions plagued by bandits, can lead his companions safely across;
so too is the Bodhisattva caravan leader, who, within the wilderness of saṃsāra and amidst the bandits of affliction, can lead all beings safely across."
"Just as a caravan leader is able to lead people out of the wilderness to save their lives, so too is the Bodhisattva;
he leads those such as the non-Buddhists, the Pāṣaṇḍas, and the Nirgranthas out of the wilderness of saṃsāra, saving their very existence."

"Furthermore, there may be kings, ministers, officials, and various sentient beings who delight in birth and death; yet, by relying upon the Bodhisattva as their great caravan leader, they too shall all attain complete salvation."

"Just as a great caravan leader, having well-prepared his provisions and necessary precious treasures, is able to lead the multitude across perilous paths and attain safety before reaching the great city;

so too is the Bodhisattva caravan leader: desiring to reach the abode of the Buddha, he travels together with a vast multitude through the perilous and remote wilderness of birth and death to reach the city on the other shore."

One should cultivate merit to adorn oneself, ensuring that meditative concentration and liberation are both fully perfected; for the Bodhisattva merchant-leader who wishes to reach the great city of omniscience, which is replete with the precious jewels of all Buddha-dharma merits.
"Just as a caravan leader gathers various precious treasures without ever feeling satisfied;
so too is the bodhisattva, gathering the treasures of the Dharma without ever feeling weary or satiated.
Just as a caravan leader skillfully guides the merchants, being preeminent in wisdom and possessing vast wealth, such that all his words are followed and put into practice by everyone."
The Bodhisattva Caravan Leader is likewise: he is the foremost guide for the multitude, his merit is immeasurable, he possesses mastery over all dharmas, and his words are non-dual.
He is well-able to lead others across perilous paths to that great city;
the Bodhisattva Caravan Leader is likewise, leading all sentient beings across the perils of birth and death, enabling them to reach the great city of nirvāṇa and the knowledge of all modes.
“Good son! One who possesses these ten things is called a bodhisattva who acts as a great caravan leader. Good son!”
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas of a bodhisattva called "skillfully knowing the path.

What are these ten? They are: knowing the level road; knowing the treacherous and evil places; knowing the secure path; knowing the insecure places; knowing the various extraordinary paths; knowing the locations of the paths; knowing the places of rest and dwelling; knowing the characteristics of the path; knowing the winding and straightness of the path; and knowing the essential exit from the path.
"Good son! To be endowed with these ten matters is called a bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of the path. Good son!"
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva knows the path without error.
What are these ten?
One should show the Mahāyāna path to those who are to be delivered; that is, one shows the Mahāyāna path and does not show the Śrāvaka path. One should show...
For those who are to be delivered by the path of the śrāvaka, he demonstrates the path of the śrāvaka and does not demonstrate the Mahāyāna path;
for those who are to be delivered by the path of omniscience (sarvākārajñatā), he demonstrates the path of omniscience and does not demonstrate the path of the śrāvaka;
for those who are to be delivered by the path of the pratyekabuddha, he demonstrates the path of the pratyekabuddha and does not demonstrate the path of omniscience.
For those who cling to the view of a self, one does not speak of emptiness and non-self;

for those who do not cling to the view of a self, one does not speak of suffering, impermanence, and non-self; for those who cling to the two extremes, one does not speak of the Middle Way; for those who cling to the Middle Way, one does not speak of the two extremes;
and for those whose minds are lost and deranged, one does not speak of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.
Furthermore, for those who have entered onto wrong paths, he explains the right path so that they may be freed from the thorns of the fetters and latent tendencies.
Son of good family,
being endowed with these ten matters is called the non-perverted path of a bodhisattva.
“Good son! Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva is said to always abide in meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
What are these ten?

He practices by contemplating the body as the foundation of mindfulness of the body; by contemplating feelings as the foundation of mindfulness of feelings; by contemplating the mind as the foundation of mindfulness of the mind; and by contemplating phenomena as the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena. He practices with a concentrated mind while dwelling in forest hermitages; he practices with a concentrated mind while contemplating the five desires; he practices with a concentrated mind while in villages, hamlets, cities, towns, kingdoms, and regions; he practices with a concentrated mind regarding fame and gain; he practices with a concentrated mind regarding the prohibitions and precepts established by the Tathāgata; and he practices with a concentrated mind regarding all places where afflictions and anger arise, as well as mental deceit and crookedness.
"How does one practice the application of mindfulness of the body (kāyasmṛtyupasthāna) to collect the mind?

By means of right wisdom, one discerns all evils and removes what is unwholesome. From the feet to the crown of the head, including the membranes of the brain, one observes that these constituent parts are devoid of self or what belongs to a self; they do not abide for even a single moment and are phenomena subject to decay. Enveloped by sinews and veins, they are foul, loathsome, and consist entirely of impure matter."

Observing in this way, one gives rise to the perception of the body as merely horizontal (transitory) and the perception of it as "mine"; through these causes and conditions and by means of these characteristics, one contemplates the marks of the body with precision, and the mind attains mastery.
"What is the application of mindfulness to feelings?
The Bodhisattva reflects thus:

'One observes that all feelings are entirely suffering; yet ordinary people and fools perversely give rise to the notion of pleasure, being ignorant and lacking wisdom, failing to discern the nature of suffering and pleasure.'"
"Worthy and noble persons observe all this as suffering; they diligently cultivate skillful means to sever and eliminate this suffering.
They also teach other sentient beings to observe sensation in this way—neither hating nor loving—and to sever all sensations.
“What is the contemplation of the station of mindfulness of the mind?

It is to contemplate the mind as impermanent yet form the notion of permanence; as suffering yet form the notion of pleasure; as non-self yet form the notion of self; and as impure yet form the notion of purity.”
The mind is like a monkey; it is as unstable as the wind, dwelling not for a single moment, swiftly changing and transforming. It is the root of the fetters and the source of the evil realms;
it constantly gives rise to flattery and crookedness, serving as the master of afflictions, and is also the causal condition for greed, hatred, and delusion.
It is the sovereign lord and craftsman of all phenomena; the mind is the precursor to all paths, and through the arising of conditions, the mind fully knows all dharmas.
The mind is like a painter who paints all manner of images yet the mind itself remains unaware;
the mind accumulates all karmas, serving as the source of both good and evil;
the mind is like a revolving cycle, like a whirling firebrand.
The mind is like the seed of fire, burning the fuel of the three realms of existence;
the mind can produce all things, just like great water.
One who observes it should know that the characteristics of the mind are the root of great affliction, and must not allow this mind to attain mastery.
If one can attain mastery over the mind, one will also attain mastery over all phenomena.
How does one contemplate the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena?

One knows unwholesome phenomena as they truly are: greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as all evil phenomena arising from their bases; one is able to cultivate the remedies for greed, hatred, and delusion, thereby severing the unwholesome.

Contemplating all wholesome dharmas with a mind that joyfully accords with them, one binds the mind in single-minded mindfulness, practices all virtues accordingly, and also teaches others to observe as one does.
How does one contemplate the five desires and practice with the mind restrained?
One does not give rise to joy or pleasure within the five desires, nor does one harbor hatred toward them;
one does not give rise to attachment toward forms, sounds, smells, tastes, or tangibles, nor does one harbor hatred toward them.

To give rise to feelings of hatred or attachment toward these phenomena that lack intrinsic substance or characteristics is to be identical to the ignorant, the common folk, infants, and the unwholesome.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One has said:

"If one conceives affection for dharmas, one also gives rise to defiled attachment; if defiled attachment arises, one becomes deluded; if delusion arises, one fails to distinguish between good and evil; by these causes and conditions, one falls into the evil realms."
Therefore, one should not feel aversion toward this dharma of emptiness;

if one feels aversion, it is called being unable to endure. If one is unable to endure, then the mind of anger increases, and one will be rebuked by one's preceptor (ācārya) and censured by fellow practitioners of the holy life (sabrahmacārin).
