If a Bodhisattva obtains gain and offerings, they do not give rise to the thought of ‘mine,’ nor do they consider the wealth and profit as belonging to themselves; furthermore, they do not conceive the thought of being the one who acquires them, nor do they form the thought of accumulating or guarding them. They constantly keep in mind giving to śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, parents, teachers and elders, kinsmen, the poor, and beggars.”
One should constantly maintain this thought:
"When food is required, I shall seek it only to sustain my life, without any mental attachment to exquisite flavors;
even if I do not obtain it, I shall neither feel distress nor give rise to feverish agitation, so as not to cause the faithful donor to lose their confidence."

If one receives lawful offerings and shares them all with the Saṃgha, the Buddha will approve such a person; the assembly of Bodhisattvas will not reproach them; the devas will constantly follow and praise them; and fellow practitioners of the holy life will have no cause for criticism or disdain. Such a person will always give rise to contentment regarding material gains and will be free from wrong livelihood.
“Good son! Possessing these ten matters is called the pure livelihood of a bodhisattva. Good son!”
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas of a bodhisattva called "freedom from weariness. What are these ten? They are:

constantly dwelling for a long time in birth and death for the sake of sentient beings without weariness in mind; being able to undergo birth and death for the sake of sentient beings; remaining free from weariness even amidst immeasurable suffering; teaching the dharma of meditative concentration to śrāvakas without giving rise to weariness; not disparaging others in mind; practicing the realization of dharmas without giving rise to weariness; possessing the dharmas of bodhi without giving rise to weariness; seeking nirvāṇa yet not realizing nirvāṇa; and flowing gradually deeper until reaching the shore of the dharma of bodhi.
"Good son! To be endowed with these ten matters is called the bodhisattva’s mind being free from weariness. Good son!"
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas for a bodhisattva called "conforming to the Buddha's teaching.

What are these ten? They are: not dwelling in states of negligence; eliminating all negligence; properly restraining the body so as not to allow the body to give rise to faults or evils; properly restraining the speech so as not to allow the speech to give rise to faults or evils; properly restraining the mind so as not to allow the mind to give rise to faults or evils; fearing the suffering of future lives and thus possessing all wholesome dharmas; practicing all wholesome dharmas and abandoning all unwholesome dharmas; preaching all wholesome dharmas and disparaging all evil dharmas; disparaging all evil karma; and practicing all wholesome karma.
One does not speak of the faults of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, extinguishes all defilements and afflictions, and guards the noble precepts established by the Tathāgata.
O son of good family!
One who possesses these ten matters is said to be a bodhisattva who accords with the Tathāgata’s teaching. “Good son,
there are further ten dharmas of a bodhisattva called ‘having a serene and joyful countenance, free from frowning.’”
What are these ten? They are: the faculties are serene and pure;

the faculties are clean and clear; the faculties are without deficiency; the faculties are free from defilement; the faculties are white and pure; one eliminates affliction and harm; one eliminates all fetters and latent tendencies; one attains the non-arising of fetters and latent tendencies; one eliminates resentment and hatred; and one remains far removed from anger.
The Bodhisattva Nivaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
As I understand what the Buddha has taught, because the sense faculties are pure, one attains a serene and joyful countenance.”
"Because one possesses a serene and pleasant countenance, one is free from all fetters and afflictions;
because one is free from all fetters and afflictions, one does not frown.
The Buddha said:
“Good son! It is so, it is so.
Your faculties are pure, your countenance is serene and joyful, you have eliminated all fetters and afflictions, and you are free from frowning.”
"Noble son!
To be endowed with these ten matters is called a bodhisattva having a serene and joyful countenance, free from frowning. Noble son!"
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva is called "learned.

What are these ten? They are: seeing the blazing of birth and death and knowing it as it truly is; seeing the blazing of malice and knowing it as it truly is; seeing the darkness and confusion of ignorance that blazes within birth and death and knowing it as it truly is; seeing that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are entirely impermanent and knowing them as they truly are; seeing that all conditioned phenomena are entirely suffering and knowing them as they truly are; seeing that the world is empty and knowing it as it truly is; seeing that all phenomena are without self and knowing them as they truly are; seeing that all sentient beings are attached to frivolous play and knowing it as it truly is; understanding that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions and knowing it as it truly is; and knowing the quiescent extinction of *nirvāṇa* as it truly is.

Relying solely on the wisdom derived from hearing and reflection, one does not grasp at mere words; having understood this, for the sake of sentient beings, one gives rise to profound great compassion and applies oneself diligently to practice with perfected vigor.
"Noble son!
Being endowed with these ten matters is called the 'much-hearing' of a bodhisattva. Noble son!"
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva is said to uphold the true Dharma. What are these ten?

When the Dharma is about to perish, the five turbidities arise; sentient beings of meager virtue mostly abide in false paths, the lamp of wisdom is about to go out, and there is no teacher capable of preaching the true Dharma.
Although the various great sūtras contain profound meanings, there is no one capable of expounding them, nor are there any who read, recite, or uphold them.

At that time, when the Dharma is in decline, the bodhisattva is able to receive and uphold the scriptural treasury (sūtrapitaka), praising it, reading and reciting it, revealing it to others, and analyzing and explaining it.

Among them, some, having heard this, gave rise to faith, confidence, and joy; they did not seek it for the sake of wealth or profit, but desired only to hear the Dharma. They conceived the thought of the World-Honored One toward the teacher of the Dharma, and the thought of nectar, the thought of immortality, and the thought of various wondrous medicines toward the Dharma they heard. Not sparing even their own bodies or lives, they diligently sought the True Dharma, and having heard it, they practiced accordingly.
"Good son! One who possesses these ten matters is called a bodhisattva who is well able to uphold the Dharma. Good son!"
Furthermore, there are ten qualities of a bodhisattva that constitute being a "Dharma Prince. What are these ten? They are: adorning the body with the perfection of the marks;

possessing the secondary signs (*anuvyañjana*) like exquisite flowers; having all faculties complete and without deficiency; being able to draw near to the teachings to which the Tathāgata has drawn near; being able to practice in accordance with the path traversed by the Tathāgata; being able to understand in accordance with the Dharma realized by the Tathāgata; bringing to maturity sentient beings who are afflicted by suffering; skillfully training in and studying the precepts; diligently practicing the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*) throughout the long night; and being able to dwell within the city where the Tathāgata resides.
"Noble son!
One who possesses these ten things is called a son of the Dharma King of the Bodhisattvas. Noble son!"
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas of a bodhisattva called "surpassing the dharmas of Śakra and the World-Protectors. What are these ten? They are: being irreversible from the bodhicitta;

being unshakable by any māras; planting all roots of goodness in the presence of all Buddhas; being able to enter the treasury of all profound dharmas; attaining the wisdom of equality regarding all dharmas; not relying on the faith of others regarding the Buddha-dharma; attaining pure wisdom; possessing dharmas not shared with śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; abiding in the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharmakṣānti); and surpassing all the dharmas of the World-Protectors.
"Noble son!
Possessing these ten things is called the Bodhisattva’s transcendence of all the dharmas of Śakra and the World-Protectors. Noble son!"
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva can know the faculties and natures of sentient beings, as well as their internal and external fetters.

What are these ten? They are: knowing, as it truly is, the nature of greed; knowing, as it truly is, the nature of hatred; knowing, as it truly is, the nature of delusion; skillfully knowing, as it truly is, the distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior, and the internal and external natures of the afflictions; skillfully knowing, as it truly is, the nature of the wholesome; skillfully knowing, as it truly is, the nature of the firm; skillfully knowing, as it truly is, the nature of the long-standing; skillfully knowing, as it truly is, the nature of the cruel and evil; and skillfully knowing the nature of a single sentient being, as well as the nature of all sentient beings in all worlds.
“Good son! Possessing these ten matters is called a bodhisattva’s skillful knowledge of the faculties and natures, as well as the internal and external fetters and afflictions. Good son!”
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas of a bodhisattva called "being able to bring sentient beings to maturity. What are these ten?
To those who should be liberated by seeing the body of a Buddha, he manifests the body of a Buddha; to those who should be liberated by seeing the body of a bodhisattva...

He immediately manifests the body of a bodhisattva for those who should be delivered by seeing the body of a bodhisattva; he manifests the body of a pratyekabuddha for those who should be delivered by seeing the body of a pratyekabuddha;
he manifests the body of a śrāvaka for those who should be delivered by seeing the body of a śrāvaka;
he manifests the body of Śakra for those who should be delivered by seeing the body of Śakra; and he manifests the body of Māra for those who should be delivered by seeing the body of Māra.
To those who should be liberated by seeing the body of a Brahmā King, he manifests the body of a Brahmā King;

to those who should be liberated by seeing the body of a Brahmin, he manifests the body of a Brahmin; to those who should be liberated by seeing the body of a Kṣatriya, he manifests the body of a Kṣatriya;
to those who should be liberated by seeing the body of a householder, he manifests the body of a householder—in this manner.
He manifests himself in whatever form is appropriate for each being. Noble son,
one who possesses these ten matters is called a bodhisattva who brings sentient beings to maturity.
“Good son! Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva is said to be well-tamed and compliant.
What are these ten?

He is upright and gentle, possessing a mind free from flattery and crookedness, a mind free from malice and harm, and a mind free from defilement; his mind is ever-pure, free from coarseness and wildness, having eliminated anger and harsh speech, and being full of patience and capable of quelling disputes.
"Noble son!
One who possesses these ten things is called a bodhisattva who is well-tamed and compliant. Noble son!"
Furthermore, there are ten qualities of a bodhisattva called dwelling in peace and harmony.

What are these ten? They are: purity of right view; being fully endowed with practice; being fully endowed with pure precepts; being fully endowed with all spheres of conduct; being in accordance with the dharma of renunciation; not dwelling within places that give rise to afflictions; having a mind that is harmonious and gentle toward fellow practitioners of the holy life (*brahmacārin*); practicing equanimity like a cow mindful of her calf; constantly delighting in the supreme right path of Bodhi; and regarding only the Buddha as venerable, seeking no other deity.
"Noble son!
Possessing these ten matters is called the Bodhisattva’s dwelling in peaceful coexistence. Noble son!"
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas for a bodhisattva called the "dharmas of integration. What are these ten? They are: integrating sentient beings through giving;

integrating sentient beings through joy; integrating sentient beings through inexhaustible giving; integrating sentient beings through benefit; integrating sentient beings through meaningful benefit; integrating sentient beings through preaching the Dharma; integrating sentient beings through transformation and guidance; integrating sentient beings by removing misfortune and bestowing profit; integrating sentient beings by sharing food and drink; and integrating sentient beings by providing all that is required for sustaining life.
"How does giving encompass sentient beings?
Constantly providing the gift of Dharma to eternally relieve their suffering—this is called giving.
How does giving bring happiness?"
To provide food so that others are at peace and free from thoughts of hunger and thirst is called the gift of happiness.
What is the inexhaustible gift?
To teach the cultivation of meditative concentration (dhyāna) so that one remains far removed from distraction is called the inexhaustible gift.
"What is the gift of benefit?
Teaching the wholesome Dharma and increasing faith is called the gift of benefit.
What is the gift of meaningful benefit?"
To teach the Dharma as it truly is and to have a profound understanding of the characteristic of emptiness is called the gift of meaningful benefit.
What is the gift of teaching the Dharma?
To rely on the sūtras and teach according to what should be heard, never speaking erroneously, is called the gift of teaching the Dharma.
"What is the gift of guidance?
To teach the Dharma as it truly is, without error or delusion—this is called the gift of guidance.
What is meant by the gift of removing misfortune and bestowing benefit?"
Diligently extinguishing unwholesome dharmas and establishing wholesome dharmas is called the gift of removing misfortune and bestowing benefit.
What is the gift of sharing food and drink?
Giving all food and drink in common with the assembly is called the gift of sharing food and drink.
"What is called the giving of necessities for sustaining life?

Elephants, horses, the seven treasures, and even all personal requisites and miscellaneous items—giving these entirely in common to the assembly is called the giving of necessities for sustaining life."
“Good son! Possessing these ten dharmas is called a bodhisattva’s practice of the methods of integration. Good son!”
Furthermore, there are ten qualities by which a bodhisattva is called handsome.

What are these ten? They are: an appearance of tranquil majesty; an appearance free from deceit and guile; a pure appearance; an appearance that inspires love and respect in those who see it; an appearance like the moon; an appearance that one never tires of beholding; an appearance that delights the mind; an appearance that everyone desires to see; an appearance that can cause all to rejoice; and an appearance that can cause all to have faith and joy.
"Noble son!
One who possesses these ten things is called an upright Bodhisattva. Noble son!"
Furthermore, there are ten qualities of a bodhisattva that are worthy of reliance. What are these ten? They are: being able to protect sentient beings so they may leave behind afflictions;

being able to cause sentient beings to emerge from the wilderness and perilous difficulties of birth and death; being able to cause sentient beings to emerge from the ocean of Māra within birth and death; being able to act as a kinsman and friend to those who have no protector; being able to act as a skilled physician for sentient beings afflicted by the disease of the defilements; being able to provide protection to those who have no protection; being able to provide a dwelling for those who have no home; being able to provide a refuge for those who have no refuge; being able to provide an island for those who have no island; and being able to lead those who have not yet reached their destination to reach it.
"Noble son!
One who possesses these ten things is called a bodhisattva who can always be relied upon. Noble son!"
Furthermore, there are ten qualities of a bodhisattva that are called the "Great Medicinal Tree.

What are these ten? For example, suppose there is a medicinal tree named "Good to Behold" (*Sudarśana*). If there are sentient beings who obtain its root, their illness is cured; those who obtain its trunk have their illness cured; those who obtain its branches have their illness cured; those who obtain its leaves have their illness cured; those who obtain its flowers have their illness cured; those who obtain its fruit have their illness cured; those who see its color have their illness cured; those who smell its fragrance have their illness cured; those who taste its flavor have their illness cured; and those who touch it have their illness cured.
"Good son!

It is the same for the bodhisattva-mahāsattva: from the first production of the thought of enlightenment, for the sake of immeasurable sentient beings who have various kinds of affliction-diseases, there are those who live by relying on renunciation, those who live by relying on precepts, those who live by relying on patience, those who live by relying on diligence, those who live by relying on meditative concentration, those who live by relying on wisdom, those who live by seeing the Dharma, those who live by hearing sounds, those who live by knowing flavors, and those who live through acting in concert."
"Good son! One who possesses these ten matters is called a bodhisattva who is like a great medicinal tree. Good son!"

Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva is said to diligently cultivate meritorious deeds. What are these ten? They are: constantly making offerings to the Triple Gem according to one’s ability;

providing medicine to those who are ill; giving food and drink to those who are hungry and thirsty; giving clothing to those seen who are naked or cold; always reverently making offerings to and receiving the instructions of one's upādhyāya and ācārya with faith; rising to welcome, reverently prostrating to, and inquiring after the welfare of fellow practitioners of the holy life (brahmacārin); constructing gardens, groves, ponds, and wells, and even bestowing grain and silk upon all; likewise equally bestowing gifts upon householders, slaves, servants, and both internal and external kin; and always being mindful to draw near to, visit, and respectfully serve śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who uphold the precepts.
"Noble son!
Possessing these ten matters is called a bodhisattva’s diligent cultivation of meritorious deeds. Noble son!"
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva is said to be skilled in performing emanations. What are these ten?
To be able to travel to all buddha-fields to inquire, question, and request instruction, while remaining unmoved in physical form within a single buddha-field; and...
Without moving from a single buddha-field, one is also able to pervade all buddha-fields to hear and receive the sublime Dharma;
without moving from a single buddha-field, one is able to universally make offerings to all Buddhas of the ten directions;
without moving from a single buddha-field, one is able to universally adorn all buddha-fields for enlightenment until they are entirely fulfilled; without moving from a single buddha-field...
Furthermore, at the time of initial enlightenment in all buddha-fields, they sit beneath the bodhi tree at the site of awakening and reverently make offerings, honor, and praise [the Buddhas];

without moving from a single buddha-field, they are able to manifest their own bodies in all buddha-lands, sitting at the sites of awakening and manifesting the attainment of the path to Buddhahood; and without moving from a single buddha-field, they are able to manifest one...
They turn the wheel of Dharma in all Buddha-fields; without moving from a single Buddha-field, they can manifest entry into nirvana in all Buddha-fields;
and without moving from a single Buddha-field, they can manifest their bodies throughout all Buddha-fields of the ten directions for those who are ready to be transformed.

Having attained the power of non-action, the bodhisattva does not form the thought of transformation nor perform transformations within any of the Buddha-lands of the ten directions; yet, according to what each sentient being ought to see, he manifests it all.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
how is it that a bodhisattva is able to perform such transformations?”
He spoke again, saying, "Do you also not form the thought of transformation, nor yet form the thought of non-transformation? "Good son!
Listen attentively now; I shall provide an analogy for you."

For example, just as the sun and moon illuminate the four continents to benefit the world, constantly bringing about profit and peace for sentient beings, yet the sun and moon do not form the thought:
"I am able to bring great benefit to all sentient beings."
"Yet all sentient beings are equally illumined by its light.

So it is with the Bodhisattva: through the causal conditions of their original virtuous karma and vows, they attain the spontaneous accomplishment of the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) state; thus, they neither conceive the thought of transformation nor perform transformations, yet they manifest transformations in every place where there is benefit."
"Good son! Being endowed with these ten matters is called the transformation of a bodhisattva. Good son!"
Furthermore, there are ten dharmas by which a bodhisattva swiftly attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
What are these ten? They are:
practicing generosity so as to bring the perfection of generosity to fulfillment;
They practice and uphold the precepts, being neither deficient in the precepts nor disparaging them; they transcend the precepts of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, fulfilling the body of pure precepts.

They fulfill patience, fulfill diligence, fulfill meditative concentration, fulfill wisdom, fulfill skillful means, fulfill vows, fulfill powers, and fulfill knowledge—surpassing all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and even bodhisattvas from the first stage up to the ninth stage, whom they cannot be reached by.
“Good son!
One who possesses these ten things is called a bodhisattva who swiftly attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
When this sutra was being spoken, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.

Within this trichiliocosm, all the various kings of mountains—the Sumeru Kings, the Mucilinda Mountains, the Mahāmucilinda Mountains, the Cakravāḍa Mountains, the Mahācakravāḍa Mountains, the jewel mountains, and the black mountains—all these mountains bowed their bodies toward Gayāśīrṣa Mountain.
Why is this? It is because of the Tathāgata’s power of sovereign supernormal faculties.
All the flowering trees, all the fruit-bearing trees, and all the fragrant trees within the trichiliocosm came forward, bending their branches toward Gayāśīrṣa Mountain.
Why is this? It is because of the Tathāgata’s power of sovereign supernormal abilities.

Immeasurable billions of nayutas of hundreds of thousands of koṭis of bodhisattvas all removed their exquisite robes and various necklaces to offer them to the Tathāgata; through his supernormal powers, these accumulated garments and necklaces of many kinds surpassed Mount Sumeru in height.

Immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of Śakras, Lokapālas, and Brahmā Kings joined their palms in prostration; they scattered mandārava flowers, mahāmandārava flowers, mañjūṣaka flowers, mahāmañjūṣaka flowers, roca flowers, and mahāroca flowers over the Buddhas.

Hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of devas in the void all scattered celestial robes and performed various musical performances; with joyful exultation, they raised a great sound and each offered celestial flowers to the Buddha, saying:

"The Buddha has appeared again in the world to turn the Wheel of Dharma once more. Sentient beings possess merit and have planted roots of virtue in the past; having long cultivated wholesome roots under former Buddhas, they are now able to hear this sutra."
"It is difficult even to hear of it, let alone to believe, understand, copy, or uphold it.

At that time, hundreds of thousands of immeasurable mahoragas produced a great thunderous sound as this Dharma was being expounded, pervading the trichiliocosm, and rained down various fragrant juices upon Mount Gayā.
Countless hundreds of thousands of nāga kings performed various musical offerings before the Buddha;
countless hundreds of thousands of gandharvas and kiṃnaras praised and made offerings with soft voices as they circumambulated Mount Gayā;
and countless hundreds of thousands of yakṣas rained down various lotus flowers and released cool, refreshing breezes.

Immeasurable hundreds of thousands of Buddhas from other directions all emitted light from the mark of the white tuft between their brows to make offerings to the Tathāgata and the Dharma he taught. This light from the white tuft manifested in various colors—blue, yellow, red, white, purple, and crystal—and circled the trichiliocosm, dispelling all darkness; it then circled Mount Gayā and vanished into the crown of the Buddha’s head.

Immeasurable hundreds of thousands of brahmins, kṣatriyas, villages, and cities offered incense, flowers, necklaces, powdered incense, robes, silk canopies, banners, and pennants as offerings to the Buddha.

While this sutra was being spoken, through such immeasurable offerings as these, seventy-two nayutas of bodhisattvas attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas; immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings were freed from all dust and defilements and attained the purity of the Dharma-eye; and immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of sentient beings resolved their minds upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The deity of Gayā Mountain, named Amṛta, together with his retinue, rose from their seats, entered his own palace, took up offerings, and made an offering to the Buddha.
Having made offerings to the Buddha, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
I recall that in the past, seventy-two thousand Buddhas all preached this sutra on this very Mount Gayā; its words and phrases were no different from those of today."
The Buddha said,
“You have gained a most excellent benefit, for you have been able to hear such a Jewel Cloud Sūtra.
At that time, there was a son of heaven who thought to himself:
“This deity of Mount Gayā has long heard this Dharma and has made offerings to seventy-two thousand buddhas; why, then, does she not transform her female body?
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Avaraṇaviṣkambhin, knowing the thoughts in that goddess’s mind, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!...”

For what reason does the goddess Amṛtā, who possesses such great spiritual power, who has heard this jewel of the Dharma, and who has made offerings to so many Buddhas, not yet transform her female body?
The Buddha replied:
"Good son, it is for the sake of benefiting sentient beings."
“By what causes and conditions is it called the inconceivable liberation? “Good son!
I recall that in the past, at the place of a Buddha named Saṃkhyeya, I saw this immortal deva deity resolve his mind upon anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”

The Immortal Deva possesses great majesty and supernormal powers; having made offerings to the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, he shall attain Buddhahood in this land, known by the name Immortal Arhat, Samyaksambuddha.
The Buddha said to Amṛta,
“Now you may manifest the buddha-field that you have accomplished.
Thereupon, the celestial deity Amṛta immediately entered the *sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi* (the samādhi that manifests all forms).

Once the Samādhi of Manifesting All Colors was attained, the ground of this trichiliocosm became as level as the palm of a hand and was entirely of deep blue lapis lazuli; all impurities and the various black mountains were completely submerged.
Everywhere one could see kalpa-trees, trees of various jewels, and trees of various fragrances;
everywhere one could see flowing springs and bathing pools, filled with water possessing the eight meritorious qualities.
All evil realms and those of lowly birth were entirely absent; in that land, even the name "woman" did not exist.
Everywhere there were lotus flowers as large as chariot wheels, upon which Bodhisattvas sat cross-legged.

That Buddha Amitāyus sat upon a lotus flower, expounding the essential teachings of the Dharma for the sake of the bodhisattvas. He was surrounded by immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of Śakras, Brahmās, and Cāturmahārājikas, and furthermore, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings all came to make offerings to the Buddha, listening attentively as he preached the Dharma in its proper sequence.
The Immortal Deva arose from the Samādhi of Manifesting All Forms, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha to the right, and immediately vanished from sight.
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
“Good sons and good daughters, how much merit must one cultivate to hear this sutra?
The Buddha said:
“If a person listens to this sutra with a sincere heart, recollects it, receives and upholds it, reads and recites it, copies it, and extensively explains it for others.”
The Buddha said:

"Furthermore, if there are sons or daughters of good family who practice giving for hundreds of thousands of billions of kalpas within this trichiliocosm, it is not equal to a son or daughter of good family who, with pure faith, copies and makes offerings [of this sutra]; because of their pure mind, they obtain far more merit."
Why is this? Material giving is slight, while the giving of the Dharma is vast.
Throughout the cycle of birth and death, sentient beings have performed immeasurable material giving within saṃsāra, yet they have never heard the gift of the supramundane Dharma.
If a son of good family or a daughter of good family were to cause all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm to establish themselves in the ten wholesome paths of action;

yet another son of good family or daughter of good family, upon hearing this True Dharma, should successively receive, uphold, read, recite, and extensively explain it to others—their merit would exceed even that of the former.
Why is this? It is because the retribution for the ten wholesome actions leads to birth in this world.

If a son or daughter of good family were to cause all sentient beings in the trichiliocosm to attain the fruit of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, arhat, or the fruit of a pratyekabuddha—even if they were to obtain such merit as this, it would still not equal hearing the meaning of a single preceding phrase, receiving and upholding it in sequence, reciting it, copying it, and explaining it extensively for others.
Why is this? Because the merits of both śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas all emerge from this sūtra.

It is by means of this sūtra that all bodhisattvas are produced, and it is through it that the Buddhas appear in the world. If one reads and recites this sūtra, and explains its sequential phrases and meanings in detail, this is itself the upholding of all Buddha-dharma.
Why is this? This sutra is the mother of all sutras; if one does not obtain this sutra, none of the great and supreme dharmas can be obtained. This sutra is the complete precepts of the bodhisattva.
All the śrāvaka disciples rose from their seats, bared their right shoulders, joined their palms, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Because we have heard this sutra within the great cycle of birth and death, we have all attained liberation."
The Buddha said: “Monk, it is so, it is so.”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly universally:
"Good sons! Good daughters!

If in any country or region there are the words, phrases, and sequential order of this sutra, you should know that such a place is itself a site of the bodhimaṇḍa, a site where the wheel of Dharma is turned, and a site of the great stūpas and images of all Buddhas; wherever this sutra exists, that is the World-Honored One himself.
Why is this? Son of good family!
Dharma is itself bodhi; Dharma is itself the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
“Good son! This Dharma is itself the Buddha; to make offerings to the Dharma is to make offerings to the Buddha.

Wherever there is a Dharma teacher who expounds the Dharma, that place is itself a stūpa. Toward this Dharma teacher, one should conceive the thought of profound reverence, the thought of a spiritual friend, and the thought of one who reveals the true path.”
Upon seeing this Dharma-preacher, one should give rise to affection, faith, reverence, and joy; one should go out to meet them from afar, invite them to take a seat, and offer praise, saying:
"Excellent, excellent! You have skillfully expounded the essential points of the Dharma."
Whether for one kalpa, or less than a kalpa, or more than a kalpa, even praising in such a manner could not exhaustively describe it. Why is this?
If there are those who delight in the Dharma, even through various forms of praise, respect, and veneration, they cannot exhaustively encompass the scope of its practice.
Even if someone were to sprinkle their own blood upon the ground, it still could not be called a complete offering of the heart.
Why is this? Such a Dharma-preacher upholds all the Buddha-seeds of the Tathāgata.
Such a Dharma-preacher should be fearless like a lion; he should not harbor thoughts of inferiority, nor should he harbor a mind of malice or harm.

Wearing clean and pure garments, one should generate deep faith and reverence; receiving praise from others, one’s mind should not become arrogant, nor should one give rise to pride or disparage others. Without seeking wealth or profit, one should preach the Dharma with single-minded devotion.
At that time, Śakra Devānām-indra addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

If there should be any world where this sutra is preached, even in its words, phrases, and sequential order, I shall personally lead my retinue to go there to make offerings and protect the Dharma-preacher.”
The Buddha said:
"Excellent, excellent, Kauśika!"
"This is what you should do.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"Regarding this sequence thus explained, what should this sutra be named? "Good son!

This sutra, by its sequence of words, phrases, and chapters, shall be named 'Jewel Cloud' (Ratnamegha); it shall also be named 'Jewel Treasury' (Ratnagarbha), also named 'Lamp of Wisdom' (Jñānapradīpa), and also named 'That Which is Upheld by the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin'."

At that time, having heard this, the Bodhisattva Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin and the other bodhisattvas, as well as the great śrāvakas, Śakra, Mahābrahmā, the World-Protecting Kings, Maheśvara, and the various sons of gods who were their leaders, down to the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, and mahoragas—an assembly of immeasurable hundreds of thousands of koṭis—all exclaimed:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Rejoicing, they practiced accordingly.
*Ratnamegha Sūtra*, Fascicle Seven.
